entries.45232d61a6008ebc3d699c0c2121c7a82d3a2626: <div sID="gen15686" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="10" osisID="Isa.10" sID="Isa.10"/> <div eID="gen15686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15687" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15688" type="x-p"/> The prophet, in this chapter, is dealing, I. With the proud oppressors of his people at home, that abused their power, to pervert justice, whom he would reckon with for their tyranny, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.1-Isa.10.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. With a threatening invader of his people from abroad, Sennacherib king of Assyria, concerning whom observe, 1. The commission given him to invade Judah, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.5-Isa.10.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>. 2. His pride and insolence in the execution of that commission, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.7-Isa.10.11">ver. 7-11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.13">13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.14">14</reference>. 3. A rebuke given to his haughtiness, and a threatening of his fall and ruin, when he had served the purposes for which God raised him up, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.12">ver. 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.15-Isa.10.19">15-19</reference>. 4. A promise of grace to the people of God, to enable them to bear up under the affliction, and to get good by it, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.20-Isa.10.23">ver. 20-23</reference>. 5. Great encouragement given to them not to fear this threatening storm, but to hope that, though for the present all the country was put into a great consternation by it, yet it would end well, in the destruction of this formidable enemy, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.24-Isa.10.34">ver. 24-34</reference>. And this is intended to quiet the minds of good people in reference to all the threatening efforts of the wrath of the church's enemies. If God be for us, who can be against us? None to do us any harm.
entries.b2826c18ce0e283295fe0d3b6d0c424a9454b9cd: <div eID="gen15688" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15687" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Condemnation of Oppressors. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 740.)</title> <div sID="gen15689" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees, and that write grievousness <hi type="italic">which</hi> they have prescribed; <hi type="super">2</hi> To turn aside the needy from judgment, and to take away the right from the poor of my people, that widows may be their prey, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> they may rob the fatherless! <hi type="super">3</hi> And what will ye do in the day of visitation, and in the desolation <hi type="italic">which</hi> shall come from far? to whom will ye flee for help? and where will ye leave your glory? <hi type="super">4</hi> Without me they shall bow down under the prisoners, and they shall fall under the slain. For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand <hi type="italic">is</hi> stretched out still. <div eID="gen15689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15690" type="x-p"/> Whether they were the princes and judges of Israel of Judah, or both, that the prophet denounced this woe against, is not certain: if those of Israel, these verses are to be joined with the close of the foregoing chapter, which is probable enough, because the burden of that prophecy (<hi type="italic">for all this his anger is not turned away</hi>) is repeated here (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.4">v. 4</reference>); if those of Judah, they then show what was the particular design with which God brought the Assyrian army upon them—to punish their magistrates for mal-administration, which they could not legally be called to account for. To them he speaks woes before he speaks comfort to God's own people. Here is, <div eID="gen15690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15691" type="x-p"/> I. The indictment drawn up against these oppressors, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.1-Isa.10.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. They are charged, 1. With making wicked laws and edicts: They <hi type="italic">decree unrighteous decrees,</hi> contrary to natural equity and the law of God: and what mischief they <hi type="italic">prescribe</hi> those under them <hi type="italic">write</hi> it, enrol it, and put it into the formality of a law. "Woe to the superior powers that devise and decree these decrees! they are not too high to be under the divine check. And woe to the inferior officers that draw them up, and enter them upon record—<hi type="italic">the writers that write the grievousness,</hi> they are not too mean to be within the divine cognizance. Principal and accessaries shall fall under the same woe." Note, It is bad to do hurt, but it is worse to do it with design and deliberation, to do wrong to many, and to involve many in the guilt of doing wrong. 2. With perverting justice in the execution of the laws that were made. No people had statutes and judgments so righteous as they had, and yet corrupt judges found ways to <hi type="italic">turn aside the needy from judgment,</hi> to hinder them from coming at their right and recovering what was their due, because they were needy and poor, and such as they could get nothing by nor expect any bribes from. 3. With enriching themselves by oppressing those that lay at their mercy, whom they ought to have protected. They make widows' houses and estates their prey, and they <hi type="italic">rob the fatherless</hi> of the little that is left them, because they have no friend to appear for them. Not to relieve them if they had wanted, not to right them if they were wronged, would have been crime enough in men that had wealth and power; but to rob them because on the side of the oppressors there was power, and the oppressed had no comforter (<reference osisRef="Eccl.4.1">Eccl. iv. 1</reference>), was such apiece of barbarity as one would think none could ever be guilty of that had either the nature of a man or the name of an Israelite. <div eID="gen15691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15692" type="x-p"/> II. A challenge given them with all their pride and power to outface the judgments of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">What will you do? To whom will you flee?</hi> You can trample upon the widows and fatherless; but <hi type="italic">what will you do when God riseth up?</hi>" <reference osisRef="Job.31.14">Job xxxi. 14</reference>. Great men, who tyrannise over the poor, think they shall never be called to account for their tyranny, shall never hear of it again, or fare the worse for it; but <hi type="italic">shall not God visit for these things?</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.5.29">Jer. v. 29</reference>. Will there not come a desolation upon those that have made others desolate? Perhaps it may <hi type="italic">come from far,</hi> and therefore may be long in coming; but it will come at last (reprieves are not pardons), and coming from far, from a quarter whence it was least expected, it will be the greater surprise and the more terrible. What will then become of these unrighteous judges? Now they <hi type="italic">see their help in the gate</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.31.21">Job xxxi. 21</reference>); but to whom will they then flee for help? Note, 1. There is a day of visitation coming, a day of enquiry and discovery, a searching day, which will bring to light, to a true light, every man, and every man's work. 2. The day of visitation will be a day of desolation to all wicked people, when all their comforts and hopes will be lost and gone, and buried in ruin, and themselves left desolate. 3. Impenitent sinners will be utterly at a loss, and will not know what to do in the day of visitation and desolation. They cannot fly and hide themselves, cannot fight it out and defend themselves; they have no refuge in which either to shelter themselves from the present evil (<hi type="italic">to whom will you flee for help?</hi>) or to secure to themselves better times hereafter: "<hi type="italic">Where will you leave your glory,</hi> to find it again when the storm is over?" The wealth they had got was their glory, and they had no place of safety in which to deposit that, but they should certainly see it flee away. If our souls be our glory, as they ought to be, and we make them our chief care, we know where to leave them, and into whose hands to commit them, even those of a faithful Creator. 4. It concerns us all seriously to consider what we shall do in the day of visitation, in a day of affliction, in the day of death and judgment, and to provide that we may do well. <div eID="gen15692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15693" type="x-p"/> III. Sentence passed upon them, by which they are doomed, some to imprisonment and captivity (<hi type="italic">they shall bow down among the prisoners,</hi> or <hi type="italic">under them</hi>—those that were most highly elevated in sin shall be most heavily loaded and most deeply sunk in trouble), others to death: they shall fall first, and so shall fall under the rest of the slain. Those that had trampled upon the widows and fatherless shall themselves be trodden down, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.4">v. 4</reference>. "This it will come to," says God, "<hi type="italic">without me,</hi> that is, because you have deserted me and driven me away from you." Nothing but utter ruin can be expected by those that live without God in the world, that cast him behind their back, and so cast themselves out of his protection. <div eID="gen15693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15694" type="x-p"/> And yet, <hi type="italic">for all this, his anger is not turned away,</hi> which intimates not only that God will proceed in his controversy with them, but that they shall be in a continual dread of it; they shall, to their unspeakable terror, see his hand still stretched out against them, and there shall remain nothing but <hi type="italic">a fearful looking for of judgment.</hi>
entries.c48025ebae0381e6b6c279d8b0a2a8f9519e12b6: <div eID="gen15694" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Pride of the King of Assyria; Sennacherib's Pride Rebuked; Destruction of the King of Assyria. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  740.)</title> <div sID="gen15695" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger, and the staff in their hand is mine indignation. <hi type="super">6</hi> I will send him against a hypocritical nation, and against the people of my wrath will I give him a charge, to take the spoil, and to take the prey, and to tread them down like the mire of the streets. <hi type="super">7</hi> Howbeit he meaneth not so, neither doth his heart think so; but <hi type="italic">it is</hi> in his heart to destroy and cut off nations not a few. <hi type="super">8</hi> For he saith, <hi type="italic">Are</hi> not my princes altogether kings? <hi type="super">9</hi> <hi type="italic">Is</hi> not Calno as Carchemish? <hi type="italic">is</hi> not Hamath as Arpad? <hi type="italic">is</hi> not Samaria as Damascus? <hi type="super">10</hi> As my hand hath found the kingdoms of the idols, and whose graven images did excel them of Jerusalem and of Samaria; <hi type="super">11</hi> Shall I not, as I have done unto Samaria and her idols, so do to Jerusalem and her idols? <hi type="super">12</hi> Wherefore it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> when the Lord hath performed his whole work upon mount Zion and on Jerusalem, I will punish the fruit of the stout heart of the king of Assyria, and the glory of his high looks. <hi type="super">13</hi> For he saith, By the strength of my hand I have done <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and by my wisdom; for I am prudent: and I have removed the bounds of the people, and have robbed their treasures, and I have put down the inhabitants like a valiant <hi type="italic">man:</hi> <hi type="super">14</hi> And my hand hath found as a nest the riches of the people: and as one gathereth eggs <hi type="italic">that are</hi> left, have I gathered all the earth; and there was none that moved the wing, or opened the mouth, or peeped. <hi type="super">15</hi> Shall the axe boast itself against him that heweth therewith? <hi type="italic">or</hi> shall the saw magnify itself against him that shaketh it? as if the rod should shake <hi type="italic">itself</hi> against them that lift it up, <hi type="italic">or</hi> as if the staff should lift up <hi type="italic">itself, as if it were</hi> no wood. <hi type="super">16</hi> Therefore shall the Lord, the Lord of hosts, send among his fat ones leanness; and under his glory he shall kindle a burning like the burning of a fire. <hi type="super">17</hi> And the light of Israel shall be for a fire, and his Holy One for a flame: and it shall burn and devour his thorns and his briers in one day; <hi type="super">18</hi> And shall consume the glory of his forest, and of his fruitful field, both soul and body: and they shall be as when a standard-bearer fainteth. <hi type="super">19</hi> And the rest of the trees of his forest shall be few, that a child may write them. <div eID="gen15695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15696" type="x-p"/> The destruction of the kingdom of Israel by Shalmaneser king of Assyria was foretold in the foregoing chapter, and it had its accomplishment in the sixth year of Hezekiah, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.10">2 Kings xviii. 10</reference>. It was total and final, head and tail were all cut off. Now the correction of the kingdom of Judah by Sennacherib king of Assyria is foretold in this chapter; and this prediction was fulfilled in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah, when that potent prince, encouraged by the successes of his predecessor against the ten tribes, <hi type="italic">came up against all the fenced cities of Judah and took them, and laid siege to Jerusalem</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.13">2 Kings xviii. 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.17">17</reference>), in consequence of which we may well suppose Hezekiah and his kingdom were greatly alarmed, though there was a good work of reformation lately begun among them: but it ended well, in the confusion of the Assyrians and the great encouragement of Hezekiah and his people in their return to God. Now let us see here, <div eID="gen15696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15697" type="x-p"/> I. How God, in his sovereignty, deputed the king of Assyria to be his servant, and made use of him as a mere tool to serve his own purposes with (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.5-Isa.10.6">v. 5, 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">O Assyrian!</hi> know this, that thou art <hi type="italic">the rod of my anger;</hi> and I will send thee to be a scourge to <hi type="italic">the people of my wrath.</hi>" Observe here, 1. How bad the character of the Jews was, though they appeared very good. They were <hi type="italic">a hypocritical nation,</hi> that made a profession of religion, and at this time particularly of reformation, but were not truly religious, not truly reformed, not so good as they pretended to be now that Hezekiah had brought goodness into fashion. When rulers are pious, and so religion is in reputation, it is common for nations to be hypocritical. They are <hi type="italic">a profane nation;</hi> so some read it. Hezekiah had in a great measure cured them of their idolatry, and now they ran into profaneness; nay, hypocrisy is profaneness: none profane the name of God so much as those who are called by that name and call upon it, and yet live in sin. Being a profane hypocritical nation, they are the people of God's wrath; they lie under his wrath, and are likely to be consumed by it. Note, Hypocritical nations are the people of God's wrath: nothing is more offensive to God than dissimulation in religion. See what a change sin made: those that had been God's chosen and hallowed people, above all people, had now become the <hi type="italic">people of his wrath.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Amos.3.2">Amos iii. 2</reference>. 2. How mean the character of the Assyrian was, though he appeared very great. He was but <hi type="italic">the rod of God's anger,</hi> an instrument God was pleased to make use of for the chastening of his people, that, being thus <hi type="italic">chastened of the Lord, they might not be condemned with the world.</hi> Note, The tyrants of the world are but the tools of Providence. Men are God's hand, his sword sometimes, to kill and slay (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.13-Ps.17.14">Ps. xvii. 13, 14</reference>), at other times his rod to correct. <hi type="italic">The staff in their hand,</hi> wherewith they smite his people, <hi type="italic">is his indignation;</hi> it is his wrath that puts the staff into their hand and enables them to deal blows at pleasure among such as thought themselves a match for them. Sometimes God makes an idolatrous nation, that serves him not at all, a scourge to a hypocritical nation, that serves him not in sincerity and truth. The Assyrian is called the <hi type="italic">rod of God's anger</hi> because he is employed by him. (1.) From him his power is derived: <hi type="italic">I will send him; I will give him a charge.</hi> Note, All the power that wicked men have, though they often use it against God, they always receive from him. Pilate could have no power against Christ unless it were <hi type="italic">given him from above,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.19.11">John xix. 11</reference>. (2.) By him the exercise of that power is directed. The Assyrian is <hi type="italic">to take the spoil and to take the prey,</hi> not to shed any blood. We read not of any slain, but he is to plunder the country, rifle the houses, drive away the cattle, strip the people of all their wealth and ornaments, and <hi type="italic">tread them down like the mire of the streets.</hi> When God's professing people wallow in the mire of sin it is just with God to suffer their enemies to tread upon them like mire. But why must the Assyrian prevail thus against them? Not that they might be ruined, but that they might be thoroughly reformed. <div eID="gen15697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15698" type="x-p"/> II. See how the king of Assyria, in his pride, magnified himself as his own master, and pretended to be absolute and above all control, to act purely according to his own will and for his own honour. <hi type="italic">God ordained him for judgment,</hi> even the <hi type="italic">mighty God established him for correction</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.12">Hab. i. 12</reference>), to be an instrument of bringing his people to repentance, <hi type="italic">howbeit he means not so, nor does his heart think so,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.10.7">v. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen15698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15699" type="x-p"/> 1. He does not think that he is either God's servant or Israel's friend, either that he <hi type="italic">can</hi> do no more than God will let him or that he <hi type="italic">shall</hi> do no more than God will make to work for the good of his people. God designs to correct his people for, and so to cure them of, their hypocrisy, and bring them nearer to himself; but was that Sennacherib's design? No, it was the furthest thing from his thoughts—<hi type="italic">he means not so.</hi> Note, (1.) The wise God often makes even the sinful passions and projects of men subservient to his own great and holy purposes. (2.) When God makes use of men as instruments in his hand to do his work it is very common for <hi type="italic">him</hi> to mean one thing and <hi type="italic">them</hi> to mean another, nay, for them to mean quite the contrary to what he intends. What Joseph's brethren designed for hurt God overruled for good, <reference osisRef="Gen.50.20">Gen. l. 20</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Mic.4.11-Mic.4.12">Mic. iv. 11, 12</reference>. Men have their ends and God has his, but we are sure <hi type="italic">the counsel of the Lord shall stand.</hi> But what is it the proud Assyrian aims at? The heart of kings is unsearchable, but God knew what was in his heart. <div eID="gen15699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15700" type="x-p"/> 2. He designs nothing but <hi type="italic">to destroy and to cut off nations not a few,</hi> and to make himself master of them. [1.] He designs to gratify his own cruelty; nothing will serve but to destroy and cut off. He hopes to regale himself with blood and slaughter; that of particular persons will not suffice, he must cut off nations. It is below him to deal by retail; he traffics in murders by wholesale. Nations, and those not a few, must have but one neck, which he will have the pleasure of cutting off. [2.] He designs to gratify his own covetousness and ambition, to set up for a universal monarch, <hi type="italic">and to gather unto him all nations,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.2.5">Hab. ii. 5</reference>. An insatiable desire of wealth and dominion is that which carries him on in this undertaking. <div eID="gen15700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15701" type="x-p"/> 3. The prophet here brings him in vaunting, and hectoring; and by his general's letter to Hezekiah, written in his name, vainglory and arrogance seem to have entered very far into the spirit and genius of the man. His haughtiness and presumption are here described very largely, and his very language copied out, partly to represent him as ridiculous and partly to assure the people of God that he would be brought down; for that maxim generally holds true, that pride goes before destruction. It also intimates that God takes notice, and keeps an account, of all men's proud and haughty words, with which they set heaven and earth at defiance. Those that speak <hi type="italic">great swelling words of vanity</hi> shall hear of them again. <div eID="gen15701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15702" type="x-p"/> (1.) He boasts of the great things he had done to other nations. [1.] He had made their kings his courtiers (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">My princes are altogether kings.</hi> Those that are now my princes are such as have been kings." Or he means that he had raised his throng to such a degree that his servants, and those that were in command under him, were as great, and lived in as much pomp, as the kings of other countries. Or those that were absolute princes in their own dominions held their crowns under him, and did him homage. This was a vainglorious boast; but how great is our God whom we serve, who is indeed King of kings, and whose subjects are made to him kings! <reference osisRef="Rev.1.6">Rev. i. 6</reference>. [2.] He had made himself master of their cities. He names several (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.9">v. 9</reference>) that were all alike reduced by him. <hi type="italic">Calno</hi> soon yielded <hi type="italic">as Carchemish</hi> did, <hi type="italic">Hamath</hi> could not hold out any more than <hi type="italic">Arpad,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Samaria</hi> had become his as well as <hi type="italic">Damascus.</hi> To support his boasts he is obliged to bring the victories of his predecessor into the account; for it was he that conquered Samaria, not Sennacherib. [3.] He had been too hard for their idols, their tutelar gods, <hi type="italic">had found out the kingdoms of the idols</hi> and found out ways to make them his own, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.10">v. 10</reference>. Their kingdoms took denomination from the idols they worshipped; the Moabites are called <hi type="italic">the people of Chemosh</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.46">Jer. xlviii. 46</reference>), because they imagined their gods were their patrons and protectors; and therefore Sennacherib vainly imagined that every conquest of a kingdom was the conquest of a god. [4.] He had enlarged his own dominions, and <hi type="italic">removed the bounds of the people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.13">v. 13</reference>), enclosing many large territories within the limits of his own kingdom and shifting a great way further the ancient land-marks which his fathers had set; he could not bear to be hemmed in so closely, but must have more room to thrive. By his <hi type="italic">removing the border of the people</hi> Mr. White understands his arbitrarily transplanting colonies from place to place, which was the constant practice of the Assyrians in all their conquests; and this is a probable interpretation. [5.] He had enriched himself with their wealth, and brought it into his own exchequer: <hi type="italic">I have robbed their treasures.</hi> In this he said truly, Great conquerors are often no better than great robbers. [6.] He had mastered all the opposition he met with: "<hi type="italic">I have put down the inhabitants as a valiant man.</hi> Those that sat high, and thought they say firmly, I have humbled and made to come down." <div eID="gen15702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15703" type="x-p"/> (2.) He boasts of the manner in which he had done them. [1.] That he had done all this by his own policy and power (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.13">v. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">By the strength of my hand,</hi> for I am valiant; <hi type="italic">and by my wisdom, for I am prudent;</hi>" not by the permission of Providence and the blessing of God. He knows not that it is God that makes him what he is, and puts the staff into his hand, but <hi type="italic">sacrifices to his own net,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.1.16">Hab. i. 16</reference>. "This wealth is all gotten by <hi type="italic">my might and the power of my hand,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Deut.8.17">Deut. viii. 17</reference>. Downright atheism and profaneness, as well as pride and vanity, are at the bottom of men's attributing their prosperity and success thus to themselves and their own conduct, and raising their own character upon it. [2.] That he had done all this with a great deal of ease, and had made but a sport and diversion of it, as if he had been taking birds' nests (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">my hand has found as a nest the riches of the people;</hi> and when he had found them there was no more difficulty in taking them than in rifling a nest, nor any more reluctance or regret within his own breast in destroying families and cities than in destroying crows'-nests; killing children was no more to him than killing birds. "<hi type="italic">As one gathers the eggs that are left</hi> in the nest by the dam, so easily <hi type="italic">have I gathered all the earth.</hi>" Like Alexander, he thought he had conquered the world; and whatever prey he seized there was none that <hi type="italic">moved the wing, or opened the mouth, or peeped,</hi> as birds do when their nests are rifled. They durst not make any opposition, no, nor any complaint; such awe did they stand in of this mighty conqueror. They were so weak that they knew it was to no purpose to resist, and he was so arbitrary that they knew it was to no purpose to complain. Strange that ever men who were made to do good should take a pride and a pleasure in doing wrong, and doing mischief to all about them without control, and should reckon that their glory which is their shame! But <hi type="italic">their</hi> day will come to fall who thus make themselves <hi type="italic">the terror of thy mighty,</hi> and much more of the feeble, <hi type="italic">in the land of the living.</hi> <div eID="gen15703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15704" type="x-p"/> (3.) He threatens what he will do to Jerusalem, which he was now about to lay siege to, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.10-Isa.10.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. He would master Jerusalem and her idols, as he had subdued other places and their idols, particularly Samaria. [1.] He blasphemously calls the God of Israel an <hi type="italic">idol,</hi> and sets him on a level with the false gods of other nations, as if none were the true God but Mithras, the sun, whom he worshipped. See how ignorant he was, and then we shall the less wonder that he was so proud. [2.] He prefers the graven images of other countries before those of Jerusalem and Samaria, when he might have known that the worshippers of the God of Israel were expressly forbidden to make any graven images, and if any did it must be by stealth, and therefore they could not be so rich and pompous as those of other nations. If he means the ark and the mercy-seat, he speaks like himself, very foolishly, and as one that judged by the sight of the eye, and might therefore be easily deceived in matters of spiritual concern. Those who make external pomp and splendour a mark of the true church go by the same rule. [3.] Because he had conquered Samaria, he concluded Jerusalem would fall of course: "<hi type="italic">Shall not I do so to Jerusalem?</hi> can I not as easily, and may I not as justly?" But it did not follow; for Jerusalem adhered to her God, whereas Samaria had forsaken him. <div eID="gen15704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15705" type="x-p"/> III. See how God, in his justice, rebukes his pride and reads his doom. We have heard what the great king, the king of Assyria, says, and how big he talks. Let us now hear what the great God has to say by his servant the prophet, and we shall find that, wherein he deals proudly, God is above him. <div eID="gen15705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15706" type="x-p"/> 1. He shows the vanity of his insolent and audacious boasts (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Shall the axe boast itself against him that hews therewith? or shall the saw magnify itself against him that draws it?</hi> So absurd are the boasts of this proud man. "O what a dust do I make!" said the fly upon the cart-wheel in the fable. "What destruction do I make among the trees!" says the axe. Two ways the axe may be said to <hi type="italic">boast itself against him that hews with it:</hi>—(1.) By way of resistance and opposition. Sennacherib blasphemed God, insulted him, threatened to serve him as he had served the gods of the nations; now this was as if the axe should fly in the face of him that hews with it. The tool striving with the workman is no less absurd than the clay striving with the potter; and as it is a thing not to be justified that men should fight against God with the wit, and wealth, and power, which he gives them, so it is a thing not to be suffered. But if men will be thus proud and daring, and bid defiances to all that is just and sacred, let them expect that God will reckon with them; the more insolent they are the surer and sorer will their ruin be. (2.) By way of rivalship and competition. Shall the axe take to itself the praise of the work it is employed in? So senseless, so absurd was it for Sennacherib to say, <hi type="italic">By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.10.13">v. 13</reference>. It is as if the rod, when it is shaken, should boast that it guides the hand which shakes it; whereas, <hi type="italic">when the staff is lifted up, is it not wood still?</hi> so the last clause may be read. If it be an ensign of authority (as the nobles of the people carried staves, <reference osisRef="Num.21.18">Num. xxi. 18</reference>), if it be an instrument of service, either to support a weak man or to correct a bad man, still it is wood, and can do nothing but as it is directed by him that uses it. The psalmist prays that God would make the nations to know that they <hi type="italic">were but men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.20">Ps. ix. 20</reference>), the staff to know that it is but wood. <div eID="gen15706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15707" type="x-p"/> 2. He foretels his fall and ruin. <div eID="gen15707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15708" type="x-p"/> (1.) That when God had done his work by him he would then do his work upon him, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.12">v. 12</reference>. For the comfort of the people of God in reference to Sennacherib's invasion, though it was a dismal time with them, let them know, [1.] That God designed to do good to Zion and Jerusalem by this providence. There is a work to be done upon them, which God intends, and which he will perform. Note, When God lets loose the enemies of his church and people, and suffers them for a time to prevail, it is in order to the performing of some great good work upon them; and, when that is done, then, and not till then, he will work deliverance for them. When God brings his people into trouble it is to try them (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.35">Dan. xi. 35</reference>), to bring sin to their remembrance and humble them for it, and to awaken them to a sense of their duty, to teach them to pray and to love and help one another; and <hi type="italic">this must be the fruit, even the taking away of sin,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.27.9">ch. xxvii. 9</reference>. When these points are, in some measure, gained by the affliction, it shall be removed, in mercy (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.41-Lev.26.42">Lev. xxvi. 41, 42</reference>), otherwise not; for, as the word, so the rod shall <hi type="italic">accomplish that for which God sends it.</hi> [2.] That when God had wrought this work of grace for his people he would work a work of wrath and vengeance upon their invaders: <hi type="italic">I will punish the fruit of the stout heart of the king of Assyria.</hi> His big words are here said to come from his stout heart, and they are the fruit of it; for <hi type="italic">out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.</hi> Notice is taken too of the <hi type="italic">glory of his high looks,</hi> for a proud look is the indication of a proud spirit. The enemies of the church are commonly very high and haughty; but, sooner or later, God will reckon for their haughtiness. He glories in it as an incontestable proof of his power and sovereignty that he <hi type="italic">looks upon proud men and abases them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.40.11">Job xl. 11</reference>, &c. <div eID="gen15708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15709" type="x-p"/> (2.) That, how threatening soever this attempt was upon Zion and Jerusalem, it should certainly be baffled, and broken, and come to nothing, and he should not be able to bring to pass his enterprise, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.16">v. 16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.19">19</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen15709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15710" type="x-p"/> [1.] Who it is that undertakes his destruction, and will be the author of it; not Hezekiah, or his princes, or the militia of Judah and Jerusalem (what can they do against such a potent force?), but God himself will do it, as <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts,</hi> and as <hi type="italic">the light of Israel. First,</hi> We are sure he can do it, for he is <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts,</hi> of all the hosts of heaven and earth. All the creatures are at his command; he makes what use he pleases on them. He is the Lord of the hosts both of Judah and of Assyria, and can give the victory to which he pleases. Let us not fear the hosts of any enemy if we have the Lord of hosts for us. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> We have reason to hope he will do it, for he is <hi type="italic">the light of Israel, and his Holy One.</hi> God is light; in him are perfect brightness, purity, and happiness. He is light, for he is the Holy One; his holiness is his glory. He is Israel's light, to direct and counsel his people, to favour and countenance them, and so to gladden and comfort them in the worst of times. He is their Holy One, for he is in covenant with them; his holiness is engaged and employed for them. God's holiness is the saints' comfort; they <hi type="italic">give thanks at the remembrance</hi> of it, and with a great deal of pleasure call him <hi type="italic">their Holy One,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.1.12">Hab. i. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen15710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15711" type="x-p"/> [2.] How this destruction is represented. It shall be, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> As a consumption of the body by a disease: <hi type="italic">The Lord shall send leanness among his fatnesses,</hi> or <hi type="italic">his fat ones.</hi> His numerous army, that was like a body covered with fatness, shall be diminished, and waste away, and become like a skeleton. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> As a consumption of buildings, or trees and bushes, by fire: <hi type="italic">Under his glory,</hi> that very thing which he glories in, <hi type="italic">he will kindle a burning, as the burning of a fire,</hi> which shall lay his army in ruins as suddenly as a raging fire lays a stately house in ashes. Some make it an allusion to the fire kindled under the sacrifices; for proud sinners fall as sacrifices to divine justice. Observe, 1. How this fire shall be kindled, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.17">v. 17</reference>. The same God that is a rejoicing light to those that serve him faithfully will be a consuming fire to those that trifle with him or rebel against him. <hi type="italic">The light of Israel shall be for a fire</hi> to the Assyrians, as the same pillar of cloud was a light to the Israelites and a terror to the Egyptians in the Red Sea. What can oppose, what can extinguish, such a fire? 2. What desolation it shall make: <hi type="italic">it shall burn and devour its thorns and briers,</hi> his officers and soldiers, which are of little worth, and vexations to God's Israel, as thorns and briers, whose end is to be burned, and which are easily and quickly consumed by a devouring fire. "<hi type="italic">Who would set the briers and thorns against me in battle?</hi> They would be so far from stopping the fire that they would inflame it. <hi type="italic">I would go through them and burn them together</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.4">ch. xxvii. 4</reference>); they shall be devoured in one day, all cut off in an instant." When they cried not only Peace and safety, but Victory and triumph, then sudden destruction came; it came surprisingly, and was completed in a little time. "Even <hi type="italic">the glory of his forest</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.18">v. 18</reference>), the choice troops of his army, the veterans, the troops of the household, the bravest regiments he had, that he was most proud of and depended most upon, that he valued as men do their timber-trees (the glory of their forest) or their fruit-trees (the glory of the Carmel), shall be put as briers and thorns before the fire; they shall be consumed both soul and body, entirely consumed, not only a limb burned, but life taken away." Note, God is able to destroy both soul and body, and therefore we should fear him more than man, who can but kill the body. Great armies before him are but as great woods, which he can fell or fire when he pleases. <div eID="gen15711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15712" type="x-p"/> [3.] What would be the effect of this great slaughter. The prophet tells us, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That the army would hereby be reduced to a very small number: <hi type="italic">The rest of the trees of his forest shall be few;</hi> very few shall escape the sword of the destroying angel, so few that there needs no artist, no muster-master or secretary of war, to take an account of them, for even <hi type="italic">a child may</hi> soon reckon the numbers of them, and <hi type="italic">write</hi> the names of <hi type="italic">them. Secondly,</hi> That those few who remained should be quite dispirited: <hi type="italic">They shall be as when a standard-bearer fainteth.</hi> When he either falls or flees, and his colours are taken by the enemy, this discourages the whole army, and puts them all into confusion. Upon the whole matter we must say, <hi type="italic">Who is able to stand before this great and holy Lord God?</hi>
entries.7eff1bc7bdedb481a6f85b3e4a7f1fce18546d3c: <div eID="gen15712" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Encouragement to Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 740.)</title> <div sID="gen15713" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> And it shall come to pass in that day, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the remnant of Israel, and such as are escaped of the house of Jacob, shall no more again stay upon him that smote them; but shall stay upon the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the Holy One of Israel, in truth. <hi type="super">21</hi> The remnant shall return, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the remnant of Jacob, unto the mighty God. <hi type="super">22</hi> For though thy people Israel be as the sand of the sea, <hi type="italic">yet</hi> a remnant of them shall return: the consumption decreed shall overflow with righteousness. <hi type="super">23</hi> For the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> of hosts shall make a consumption, even determined, in the midst of all the land. <div eID="gen15713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15714" type="x-p"/> The prophet had said (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.12">v. 12</reference>) that <hi type="italic">the Lord would perform his whole work upon Mount Zion and upon Jerusalem,</hi> by Sennacherib's invading the land. Now here we are told what that work should be, a twofold work:— <div eID="gen15714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15715" type="x-p"/> I. The conversion of some, to whom this providence should be sanctified and yield the peaceable fruit of righteousness, though for the present it was not joyous, but grievous; these are but a remnant (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.22">v. 22</reference>), <hi type="italic">the remnant of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.20">v. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">the remnant of Jacob</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.21">v. 21</reference>), but a very few in comparison with the vast numbers of the people of Israel, who were as the sand of the sea. Note, Converting work is wrought but on a remnant, who are distinguished from the rest and set apart for God. When we see how populous Israel is, how numerous the members of the visible church are, as the sand of the sea, and yet consider that of these a remnant only shall be saved, that of the many that are called there are but few chosen, we shall surely <hi type="italic">strive to enter in at the strait gate</hi> and fear lest we <hi type="italic">seem to come short.</hi> This remnant of Israel are said to be <hi type="italic">such as had escaped of the house of Jacob,</hi> such as escaped the corruptions of the house of Jacob, and kept their integrity in times of common apostasy; and that was a fair escape. And therefore they escape the desolations of that house, and shall be preserved in safety in times of common calamity; and that also will be a fair and narrow escape. Their <hi type="italic">lives shall be given them for a prey,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.45.5">Jer. xlv. 5</reference>. The <hi type="italic">righteous scarcely are saved.</hi> Now, 1. This remnant shall come off from all confidence in an arm of flesh, this providence shall cure them of that: "They <hi type="italic">shall no more again stay upon him that smote them,</hi> shall never depend upon the Assyrians, as they have done, for help against their other enemies, finding that they are themselves their worst enemies." <hi type="italic">Ictus piscator sapit—sufferings teach caution.</hi> "They have now learned by dear-bought experience the folly of leaning upon that staff as a stay to them which may perhaps prove a staff to beat them." It is part of the covenant of a returning people (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.3">Hos. xiv. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">Assyria shall not save us.</hi> Note, By our afflictions we may learn not to make creatures our confidence. 2. They shall come home to God, to the mighty God (one of the names given to the Messiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">ch. ix. 6</reference>), to the Holy One of Israel: "<hi type="italic">The remnant shall return</hi> (that was signified by the name of the prophet's son, <hi type="italic">Shear-jashub,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.7.3">ch. vii. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">even the remnant of Jacob.</hi> They shall return, after the raising of the siege of Jerusalem, not only to the quiet possession of their houses and lands, but to God and to their duty; they shall repent, and pray, and seek his face, and reform their lives." The remnant that escape are a returning remnant: they shall return to God, and shall stay upon him. Note, Those only may with comfort stay upon God that return to him; then may we have a humble confidence in God when we make conscience of our duty to him. They <hi type="italic">shall stay upon the Holy One of Israel, in truth,</hi> and not in pretence and profession only. This promise of the conversion and salvation of a remnant of Israel is applied by the apostle (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.27">Rom. ix. 27</reference>) to the remnant of the Jews which at the first preaching of the gospel received and entertained it, and sufficiently proves that it was no new thing for God to abandon to ruin a great many of the seed of Abraham in full force and virtue; for so it was now. The number of the children of Israel was <hi type="italic">as the sand of the sea</hi> (according to the promise, <reference osisRef="Gen.22.17">Gen. xxii. 17</reference>), and yet only a remnant shall be saved. <div eID="gen15715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15716" type="x-p"/> II. The consumption of others: <hi type="italic">The Lord God of hosts shall make a consumption,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.10.23">v. 23</reference>. This is not meant (as that <reference osisRef="Isa.10.18">v. 18</reference>) of the consumption of the Assyrian army, but of the consumption of the estates and families of many of the Jews by the Assyrian army. This is taken notice of to magnify the power and goodness of God in the escape of the distinguished remnant, and to let us know what shall become of those that will not return to God; they shall be wasted away by this consumption, this general decay <hi type="italic">in the midst of the land.</hi> Observe, 1. It is a consumption of God's own making; he is the author of it. The Lord God of hosts, whom none can resist, shall make this consumption. 2. It is <hi type="italic">decreed.</hi> It is not the product of a sudden resolve, but was before ordained. It is <hi type="italic">determined,</hi> not only that there shall be such a consumption, but it is <hi type="italic">cut out</hi> (so the word is); it is particularly appointed how far it shall extend and how long it shall continue, who shall be consumed by it and who not. 3. It is an overflowing consumption, that shall overspread the land, and, like a mighty torrent or inundation, bear down all before it. 4. Though it overflows, it is not at random, but in <hi type="italic">righteousness,</hi> which signifies both wisdom and equity. God will justly bring this consumption upon a provoking people, but he will wisely and graciously set bounds to it. <hi type="italic">Hitherto it shall come, and no further.</hi>
entries.14703a7e009f88ef1fb4c2833bc7e2d5c8f0145b: <div eID="gen15716" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Encouragement to Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 740.)</title> <div sID="gen15717" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> Therefore thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> of hosts, O my people that dwellest in Zion, be not afraid of the Assyrian: he shall smite thee with a rod, and shall lift up his staff against thee, after the manner of Egypt. <hi type="super">25</hi> For yet a very little while, and the indignation shall cease, and mine anger in their destruction. <hi type="super">26</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts shall stir up a scourge for him according to the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb: and <hi type="italic">as</hi> his rod <hi type="italic">was</hi> upon the sea, so shall he lift it up after the manner of Egypt. <hi type="super">27</hi> And it shall come to pass in that day, <hi type="italic">that</hi> his burden shall be taken away from off thy shoulder, and his yoke from off thy neck, and the yoke shall be destroyed because of the anointing. <hi type="super">28</hi> He is come to Aiath, he is passed to Migron; at Michmash he hath laid up his carriages: <hi type="super">29</hi> They are gone over the passage: they have taken up their lodging at Geba; Ramah is afraid; Gibeah of Saul is fled. <hi type="super">30</hi> Lift up thy voice, O daughter of Gallim: cause it to be heard unto Laish, O poor Anathoth. <hi type="super">31</hi> Madmenah is removed; the inhabitants of Gebim gather themselves to flee. <hi type="super">32</hi> As yet shall he remain at Nob that day: he shall shake his hand <hi type="italic">against</hi> the mount of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem. <hi type="super">33</hi> Behold, the Lord, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, shall lop the bough with terror: and the high ones of stature <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> hewn down, and the haughty shall be humbled. <hi type="super">34</hi> And he shall cut down the thickets of the forest with iron, and Lebanon shall fall by a mighty one. <div eID="gen15717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15718" type="x-p"/> The prophet, in his preaching, distinguishes between the precious and the vile; for God in his providence, even in the same providence, does so. He speaks terror, in Sennacherib's invasion, to the hypocrites, who were the <hi type="italic">people of God's wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.10.6">v. 6</reference>. But here he speaks comfort to the sincere, who were the people of God's love. The judgment was sent for the sake of the former; the deliverance was wrought for the sake of the latter. Here we have, <div eID="gen15718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15719" type="x-p"/> I. An exhortation to God's people not to be frightened at this threatening calamity, nor to be put into any confusion or consternation by it. <hi type="italic">Let the sinners in Zion be afraid</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.14">ch. xxxiii. 14</reference>): but <hi type="italic">O my people, that dwellest in Zion, be not afraid of the Assyrian,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.10.24">v. 24</reference>. Note, It is against the mind and will of God that his people, whatever may happen, should give way to that fear which has torment and amazement. Those that dwell in Zion, where God dwells and where his people attend him, and are employed in his service, that are under the protection of the bulwarks that are <hi type="italic">round about Zion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.48.13">Ps. xlviii. 13</reference>), need not be afraid of any enemy. Let their souls dwell at ease in God. <div eID="gen15719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15720" type="x-p"/> II. Considerations offered for the silencing of their fear. <div eID="gen15720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15721" type="x-p"/> 1. The Assyrian shall do nothing against them but what God has appointed and determined. They are here told before hand what he shall do, that it may be no surprise to them: "<hi type="italic">He shall smite thee</hi> by the divine permission, but it shall be only <hi type="italic">with a rod</hi> to correct thee, not with a sword to wound and kill; nay, <hi type="italic">he shall but lift up his staff against thee,</hi> threaten thee, and frighten thee, and shake the rod at thee, <hi type="italic">after the manner of Egypt,</hi> as the Egyptians shook their staff against your fathers at the Red Sea, when they said, <hi type="italic">We will pursue, we will overtake</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.9">Exod. xv. 9</reference>), but could not reach to do them any hurt." Note, We should not be frightened at those enemies that can do no more than frighten us. <div eID="gen15721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15722" type="x-p"/> 2. The storm shall soon blow over (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">Yet a very little while—a little, little while</hi> (so the word is), <hi type="italic">and the indignation shall cease, even my anger,</hi> which is <hi type="italic">the staff in their hand</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">v. 5</reference>), so that when that ceases they are disarmed and disabled to do any further mischief. Note, God's anger against his people is but for a moment (<reference osisRef="Ps.30.5">Ps. xxx. 5</reference>), and when that ceases, and is turned away from us, we need not fear the fury of any man, for it is impotent passion. <div eID="gen15722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15723" type="x-p"/> 3. The enemy that threatens them shall himself be reckoned with. God's anger against his people <hi type="italic">shall cease in the destruction</hi> of their enemies; when he turns away his wrath from Israel he shall turn it against the Assyrian; and the rod with which he corrected his people shall not only be laid aside, but thrown into the fire. He <hi type="italic">lifted up his staff</hi> against Zion, but God <hi type="italic">shall stir up a scourge for him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.26">v. 26</reference>); he is a terror to God's people, but God will be a terror to him. The destroying angel shall be this scourge, which he can neither flee from nor contend with. The prophet, for the encouragement of God's people, quotes precedents, and puts them in mind of what God had done formerly against the enemies of his church, who were very strong and formidable, but were brought to ruin. The destruction of the Assyrian shall be, (1.) <hi type="italic">According to the slaughter of Midian</hi> (which was effected by an invisible power, but effected suddenly, and it was a total rout); and as, <hi type="italic">at the rock of Oreb,</hi> one of the princes of Midian, after the battle, was slain, so shall Sennacherib be in the temple of his god Nisroch, after the defeat of his forces, when he thinks the bitterness of death is past. Compare with this <reference osisRef="Ps.83.11">Ps. lxxxiii. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">Make their nobles like Oreb and like Zeeb;</hi> and see how God's promises and his people's prayers agree. (2.) <hi type="italic">As his rod was upon the sea,</hi> the Red Sea, as Moses' rod was upon that, to divide it first for the escape of Israel and then to close it again for the destruction of their pursuers, so shall his rod now be <hi type="italic">lifted up, after the manner of Egypt,</hi> for the deliverance of Jerusalem and the destruction of the Assyrian. Note, It is good to observe a resemblance between God's latter and former appearances for his people, and against his and their enemies. <div eID="gen15723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15724" type="x-p"/> 4. They shall be wholly delivered from the power of the Assyrian, and from the fear of it, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.27">v. 27</reference>. "They shall not only be eased of the Assyrian army, which is now quartered upon them and which is a grievous yoke and burden to them, but they shall no more pay that tribute to the king of Assyria which before this invasion he exacted from them (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.14">2 Kings xviii. 14</reference>), shall be no longer at his service, nor lie at his mercy, as they have done; nor shall he ever again put the country under contribution." Some think it looks further, to the deliverance of the Jews out of their captivity in Babylon; and further yet, to the redemption of believers from the tyranny of sin and Satan. The yoke shall not only be taken away, but it <hi type="italic">shall be destroyed.</hi> The enemy shall no more recover his strength, to do the mischief he has done; and this <hi type="italic">because of the anointing,</hi> for their sakes who were partakers of the anointing. (1.) For Hezekiah's sake, who was the anointed of the Lord, who had been an active reformer, and was dear to God. (2.) For David's sake. This is particularly given as the reason why God would defend Jerusalem from Sennacherib (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.35">ch. xxxvii. 35</reference>), <hi type="italic">For my own sake, and for my servant David's sake.</hi> (3.) For his people Israel's sake, the good people among them that had received the unction of divine grace. (4.) For the sake of the Messiah, the Anointed of God, whom God had an eye to in all the deliverances of the Old-Testament church, and hath still an eye to in all the favours he shows to his people. It is for his sake that the yoke is broken, and that we are made free indeed. <div eID="gen15724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15725" type="x-p"/> III. A description both of the terror of the enemy and the terror with which many were struck by it, and the folly of both exposed, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.28-Isa.10.34">v. 28</reference>, to the end. Here observe, <div eID="gen15725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15726" type="x-p"/> 1. How formidable the Assyrians were and how daring and threatening they affected to appear. Here is a particular description of the march of Sennacherib, what course he steered, what swift advances he made: <hi type="italic">He has come to Aiath,</hi> &c. "This and the other place he has made himself master of, and has met with no opposition." <hi type="italic">At Michmash he has laid up his carriages,</hi> as if he had no further occasion for his heavy artillery, so easily was every place he came to reduced; or the store-cities of Judah, which were fortified for that purpose, had now become his magazines. Some remarkable pass, and an important one, he had taken: <hi type="italic">They have gone over the passage.</hi> <div eID="gen15726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15727" type="x-p"/> 2. How cowardly the men of Judah were, the degenerate seed of that lion's whelp. They were <hi type="italic">afraid;</hi> they <hi type="italic">fled</hi> upon the first alarm, and did not offer to make any head against the enemy. Their apostasy from God had dispirited them, so that one chased a thousand of them. Instead of a valiant shout, to animate one another, nothing was heard by lamentation, to discourage and weaken one another. And <hi type="italic">poor Anathoth,</hi> a priests' city, that should have been a pattern of courage, shrieks louder than any, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.30">v. 30</reference>. With respect to those that <hi type="italic">gathered themselves</hi> together, it was not to fight, but to flee by consent, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.31">v. 31</reference>. This is designed either, (1.) To show how fast the news of the enemy's progress flew through the kingdom: <hi type="italic">He has come to Aiath,</hi> says one; nay, says another, <hi type="italic">He has passed to Migron,</hi> &c. And yet, perhaps, it was not altogether so bad as common fame represented it. But we must watch against the fear, not only of evil things, but of evil tidings, which often make things worse than really they are, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.7">Ps. cxii. 7</reference>. Or, (2.) To show what imminent danger Jerusalem was in, when its enemies made so many bold advances towards it and its friends could not make one bold stand to defend it. Note, The more daring the church's enemies are, and the more dastardly those are that should appear for her, the more will God be exalted in his own strength, when, notwithstanding this, he works deliverance for her. <div eID="gen15727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15728" type="x-p"/> 3. How impotent his attempt upon Jerusalem shall be: <hi type="italic">he shall remain at Nob,</hi> whence he may see Mount Zion, and there <hi type="italic">he shall shake his hand</hi> against it, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.32">v. 32</reference>. He shall threaten it, and that shall be all; it shall be safe, and shall set him at defiance. The daughter of Jerusalem, to be even with him, shall <hi type="italic">shake her head</hi> at him, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.22">ch. xxxvii. 22</reference>. <div eID="gen15728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15729" type="x-p"/> 4. How fatal it would prove, in the issue, to himself. When he <hi type="italic">shakes his hand at Jerusalem,</hi> and is about to lay hands on it, then is God's time to appear against him; for Zion is the place of which God has said, <hi type="italic">This is my rest for ever;</hi> therefore those who threaten it affront God himself. Then <hi type="italic">the Lord shall lop the bough with terror and cut down the thickets of the forest,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.10.33-Isa.10.34">v. 33, 34</reference>. (1.) The pride of the enemy shall be humbled, the boughs that are lifted up on high shall be lopped off, the high and stately trees shall be hewn down; that is, the haughty shall be humbled. Those that lift up themselves in competition with God or opposition to him shall be abased. (2.) The power of the enemy shall be broken: <hi type="italic">The thickets of the forest he shall cut down.</hi> When the Assyrian soldiers were under their arms, and their spears erect, they looked like a forest, like Lebanon; but, when in one night they all became as dead corpses, the pikes were laid on the ground, and Lebanon was of a sudden cut down <hi type="italic">by a mighty one,</hi> by the destroying angel, who in a little time slew so many thousands of them: and, if this shall be the exit of that proud invader, let not God's people be afraid of him. <hi type="italic">Who art thou, that thou shouldst be afraid of a man that shall die?</hi>  <chapter eID="Isa.10"/> <div eID="gen15729" type="x-p"/>

entries.b02e8bae06b1efdfe1e4fb7372afb81ff33c5dbe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8494"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 10</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.10.1-Isa.10.4">Is 10:1-4</reference>. Fourth strophe.</title> <div sID="gen13778" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8494"/><hi type="bold">1. them that decree--</hi>namely, unrighteous judges.<div eID="gen13778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13779" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">write grievousness, &c.--</hi>not the scribes, but the magistrates who caused unjust decisions (literally, "injustice" or "grievousness") to be recorded by them (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.6">Is 65:6</reference>) [Maurer], (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.10">Is 1:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.23">23</reference>). <div eID="gen13779" type="x-p"/>
entries.1300a35f7a4e3e951d58bb87e728e624820d84a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8495"/><div sID="gen13780" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8495"/><hi type="bold">2. To turn aside, &c.--</hi>The effect of their conduct is to pervert the cause of the needy [Horsley]. In English Version "from judgment" means "from obtaining justice."<div eID="gen13780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13781" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">take away the right--</hi>"make plunder of the right" (rightful claim) [Horsley]. <div eID="gen13781" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a752336909cd0efc8d893801d2a94d86a5ab28e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8496"/><div sID="gen13782" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8496"/><hi type="bold">3. what will ye do--</hi>what way of escape will there be for you?<div eID="gen13782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13783" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">visitation--</hi>of God's wrath (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.14">Is 26:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.35.15">Job 35:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.9.7">Ho 9:7</reference>).<div eID="gen13783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13784" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from far--</hi>from Assyria.<div eID="gen13784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13785" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">leave ... glory--</hi>rather, "deposit (for safekeeping) your wealth" [Lowth]. So <reference osisRef="Ps.49.17">Psa 49:17</reference>. <div eID="gen13785" type="x-p"/>
entries.77a8bd6c4e7fcaab745762fbc84ba9bf4bb2ee73: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8497"/><div sID="gen13786" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8497"/><hi type="bold">4. Without me--</hi>not having Me to "flee to" (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.3">Is 10:3</reference>).<div eID="gen13786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13787" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bow down--</hi>Bereft of strength they shall fall; or else, they shall lie down fettered.<div eID="gen13787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13788" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">under ... under--</hi>rather, "among" (literally, "in the place of") [Horsley]. The "under" may be, however, explained, "trodden under the (feet of the) prisoners going into captivity," and "overwhelmed under the heaps of slain on the battlefield" [Maurer].<div eID="gen13788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13789" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.10.5-Isa.10.34">Is 10:5-34</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.11.12">Is 11:12</reference>. Destruction of the Assyrians; Coming of Messiah; Hymn of Praise.<div eID="gen13789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13790" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.10.9">Is 10:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.11">11</reference> show that Samaria was destroyed before this prophecy. It was written when Assyria proposed (a design which it soon after tried to carry out under Sennacherib) to destroy Judah and Jerusalem, as it had destroyed Samaria. This is the first part of Isaiah's prophecies under Hezekiah. Probably between 722 and 715 B.C. (see <reference osisRef="Isa.10.27">Is 10:27</reference>). <div eID="gen13790" type="x-p"/>
entries.b0ac4d59212595f68b56ac41f2976363dab9805b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8498"/><div sID="gen13791" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8498"/><hi type="bold">5. O Assyrian, &c.--</hi>rather, "What, ho (but Maurer, Woe to the) Assyrian! He is the rod and staff of Mine anger (My instrument in punishing, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.20">Jr 51:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.17.13">Psa 17:13</reference>). In their hands is Mine indignation" [Horsley, after Jerome]. I have put into the Assyrians' hands the execution of Mine indignation against My people. <div eID="gen13791" type="x-p"/>
entries.a85d0a0661f9c0e2cb45162afef8308b69ed8869: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8499"/><div sID="gen13792" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8499"/><hi type="bold">6. send him--</hi>"Kings' hearts are in the hand of the Lord" (<reference osisRef="Prov.21.1">Pr 21:1</reference>).<div eID="gen13792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13793" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hypocritical--</hi>polluted [Horsley].<div eID="gen13793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13794" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nation--</hi>Judah, against whom Sennacherib was forming designs.<div eID="gen13794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13795" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of my wrath--</hi>objects of My wrath.<div eID="gen13795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13796" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">give ... charge--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.34.22">Jr 34:22</reference>).<div eID="gen13796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13797" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and to tread, &c.--</hi>Horsley translates: "And then to make him (the Assyrian) a trampling under foot like the mire of the streets" (so <reference osisRef="Isa.10.12">Is 10:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Is 33:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.10.5">Zec 10:5</reference>). But see <reference osisRef="Isa.37.26">Is 37:26</reference>. <div eID="gen13797" type="x-p"/>
entries.631f6894b3c5b4e7190a9a94e9a920f5e73748d8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8500"/><div sID="gen13798" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8500"/><hi type="bold">7. meaneth not so--</hi>He is only thinking of his own schemes, while God is overruling them to His purposes.<div eID="gen13798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13799" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">think--</hi>intend. Sinners' plans are no less culpable, though they by them unconsciously fulfil God's designs (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.10">Psa 76:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.4.12">Mi 4:12</reference>). So Joseph's brethren (<reference osisRef="Gen.50.20">Ge 50:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.16.4">Pr 16:4</reference>). The sinner's motive, not the result (which depends on God), will be the test in judgment.<div eID="gen13799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13800" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heart to destroy ... not a few--</hi>Sennacherib's ambition was not confined to Judea. His plan was also to conquer Egypt and Ethiopia (<reference osisRef="Isa.20.1-Isa.20.6">Is 20:1-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.1.15">Zec 1:15</reference>). <div eID="gen13800" type="x-p"/>
entries.77a212136a040276d41dca232c1e1c5d885a660b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8501"/><div sID="gen13801" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8501"/>8-11. Vauntings of the Assyrians. Illustrated by the self-laudatory inscriptions of Assyria deciphered by Hincks.<div eID="gen13801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13802" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">princes ... kings--</hi>Eastern satraps and governors of provinces often had the title and diadem of kings. Hence the title, "King of kings," implying the greatness of Him who was over them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.7">Eze 26:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.12">Ezr 7:12</reference>). <div eID="gen13802" type="x-p"/>
entries.4a9d1e18e0ca27bea5cd433096c87df894ad9ea4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8504"/><div sID="gen13814" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8504"/><hi type="bold">12. whole work--</hi>His entire plan is regard to the punishment of the Jews (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.5-Isa.10.7">Is 10:5-7</reference>).<div eID="gen13814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13815" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zion--</hi>the royal residence, the court, princes and nobles; as distinguished from "Jerusalem," the people in general.<div eID="gen13815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13816" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fruit--</hi>the result of, that is, the plants emanating from.<div eID="gen13816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13817" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stout--</hi>Hebrew, "greatness of," that is, pride of.<div eID="gen13817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13818" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">glory--</hi>haughtiness. <div eID="gen13818" type="x-p"/>
entries.077eee829e1ed98744e80423a5df37785cf8dcb8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8505"/><div sID="gen13819" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8505"/><hi type="bold">13. I am prudent--</hi>He ascribes his success to his own prudence, not to God's providence.<div eID="gen13819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13820" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">removed the bounds--</hi>set aside old, and substituted new boundaries of kingdoms at will. A criminal act, as Jehovah Himself had appointed the boundaries of the nations (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.8">De 32:8</reference>).<div eID="gen13820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13821" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">treasures--</hi>"hoarded treasures" [Horsley].<div eID="gen13821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13822" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">put down ... inhabitants like, &c.--</hi>rather, "as a valiant man, I have brought down (from their seats) those seated" (namely, "on thrones"; as in <reference osisRef="Ps.2.4">Psa 2:4</reference>; 29:10; 55:19). The Hebrew for "He that abideth," is He that sitteth on a throne); otherwise, "I have brought down (as captives into Assyria, which lay lower than Judea; therefore 'brought down,' compare <reference osisRef="Isa.36.1">Is 36:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.36.10">10</reference>), the inhabitants" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen13822" type="x-p"/>
entries.225cf486444054504654b5f3d3bdecf3ae90b268: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8506"/><div sID="gen13823" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8506"/><hi type="bold">14. nest--</hi>implying the ease with which he carried off all before him.<div eID="gen13823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13824" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">left--</hi>by the parent bird.<div eID="gen13824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13825" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">none ... moved ... wing--</hi>image from an angry bird resisting the robbery of its "nest."<div eID="gen13825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13826" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">peeped--</hi>chirped even low (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.19">Is 8:19</reference>). No resistance was offered me, of deed, or even word. <div eID="gen13826" type="x-p"/>
entries.c22e81dc61f72320796dd9d9186cfa2d61329bf3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8507"/><div sID="gen13827" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8507"/>15. Shall the instrument boast against Him who uses it? Through free in a sense, and carrying out his own plans, the Assyrian was unconsciously carrying out God's purposes.<div eID="gen13827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13828" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shaketh it--</hi>moves it back and forward.<div eID="gen13828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13829" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">staff ... lift ... itself ... no wood--</hi>rather, "as if the staff (man, the instrument of God's judgments on his fellow man) should set aside (Him who is) not wood" (not a mere instrument, as man). On "no wood" compare <reference osisRef="Deut.32.21">De 32:21</reference>, "that which is not God;" <reference osisRef="Isa.31.8">Is 31:8</reference> shows that God is meant here by "not wood" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen13829" type="x-p"/>
entries.87567b88a394de81f9c61bf6382cb36e63d516f8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8508"/><div sID="gen13830" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8508"/><hi type="bold">16. fat ones--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.5.17">Is 5:17</reference>). The robust and choice soldiers of Assyria (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.31">Psa 78:31</reference>, where "fattest" answers in the parallelism to "chosen," or "young men," Margin).<div eID="gen13830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13831" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">leanness--</hi>carrying out the image on "fat ones." Destruction (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.15">Psa 106:15</reference>). Fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.36">Is 37:36</reference>).<div eID="gen13831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13832" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his glory--</hi>Assyria's nobles. So in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.13">Is 5:13</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.7">Is 8:7</reference>.<div eID="gen13832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13833" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kindle--</hi>a new image from fire consuming quickly dry materials (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.6">Zec 12:6</reference>). <div eID="gen13833" type="x-p"/>
entries.cbd5fd7292c6d20f6537cc902e19801a498e16f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8509"/><div sID="gen13834" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8509"/><hi type="bold">17-18. light of Israel--</hi>carrying out the image in the end of <reference osisRef="Isa.10.16">Is 10:16</reference>. Jehovah, who is a light to Israel, shall be the "fire" (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.24">De 4:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.29">He 12:29</reference>) that shall ignite the "thorns," (the Assyrians, like dry fuel, a ready prey to flame). <div eID="gen13834" type="x-p"/>
entries.28ee37e0b6b0a06eed3ce5fe832e11a3eecfa500: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8511"/><div sID="gen13840" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8511"/><hi type="bold">19. rest--</hi>those who shall survive the destruction of the host.<div eID="gen13840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13841" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his forest--</hi>same image as in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.18">Is 10:18</reference>, for the once dense army.<div eID="gen13841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13842" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">child ... write--</hi>so few that a child might count them. <div eID="gen13842" type="x-p"/>
entries.680f4de270584b99390e380975566a56a59445f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8512"/><div sID="gen13843" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8512"/>20-22. The effect on the "remnant" (contrasted with the Assyrian remnant, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.19">Is 10:19</reference>); namely, those who shall be left after the invasion of Sennacherib, will be a return from dependence on external idolatrous nations, as Assyria and Egypt (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.21">2Ki 18:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.7-2Kgs.16.9">16:7-9</reference>), to the God of the theocracy; fulfilled in part in the pious Hezekiah's days; but from the future aspect under which Paul, in <reference osisRef="Rom.9.27">Ro 9:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.28">28</reference> (compare "short work" with "whole work," <reference osisRef="Isa.10.12">Is 10:12</reference>, here), regards the whole prophecy, the "remnant," "who stay upon the Lord," probably will receive their fullest realization in the portion of Jews left after that Antichrist shall have been overthrown, who shall "return" unto the Lord (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.13">Is 6:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.7.3">7:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.12.9">Zec 12:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.2">14:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.12">Zep 3:12</reference>). <div eID="gen13843" type="x-p"/>
entries.abc14f2ac86a7dbd8fb81ea12f1e343d2950b85a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8515"/><div sID="gen13846" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8515"/><hi type="bold">23. even determined--</hi>"A consumption, and whatever is determined," or decreed [Maurer].<div eID="gen13846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13847" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">midst--</hi>Zion, the central point of the earth as to Jehovah's presence.<div eID="gen13847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13848" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">land--</hi>Israel. But the Septuagint, "in the whole habitable world." So English Version (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.28">Ro 9:28</reference>), "upon the earth." <div eID="gen13848" type="x-p"/>
entries.a44af672ca246e81c43e5912e50b377d79c66c60: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8516"/><div sID="gen13849" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8516"/><hi type="bold">24. Therefore--</hi>Return to the main proposition, Assyria's ultimate punishment, though employed as God's "rod" to chastise Judea for a time.<div eID="gen13849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13850" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">O my people--</hi>God's tenderness towards His elect nation.<div eID="gen13850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13851" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after the manner of Egypt--</hi>as Egypt and Pharaoh oppressed thee. Implying, too, as Israel was nevertheless delivered from them, so now it would be from the Assyrian Sennacherib. The antithesis in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.26">Is 10:26</reference> requires this interpretation [Maurer]. <div eID="gen13851" type="x-p"/>
entries.fce97deaf364e411325e1540d691404d063dcf4a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8517"/><div sID="gen13852" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8517"/><hi type="bold">25. For--</hi>Be not afraid (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.24">Is 10:24</reference>), for, &c.<div eID="gen13852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13853" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">indignation ... cease--</hi>The punishments of God against Israel shall be consummated and ended (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.20">Is 26:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.36">Da 11:36</reference>). "Till the indignation be accomplished," &c.<div eID="gen13853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13854" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mine anger--</hi>shall turn to their (the Assyrians') destruction. <div eID="gen13854" type="x-p"/>
