entries.6775b83e758b4e460a1721e21e37f9e879d70eb0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8518"/><div sID="gen13855" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8518"/><hi type="bold">26. slaughter of--</hi>"stroke upon."<div eID="gen13855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13856" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Midian--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.9.4">Is 9:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.7.25">Jud 7:25</reference>).<div eID="gen13856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13857" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as his rod was upon the sea--</hi>rather, understanding "stroke" from the previous clause, "according to the stroke of His rod upon the Red Sea" (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.16">Ex 14:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.14.26">26</reference>). His "rod" on the Assyrian (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.24">Is 10:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.26">26</reference>) stands in bold contrast to the Assyrian used as a "rod" to strike others (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">Is 10:5</reference>).<div eID="gen13857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13858" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after the manner of Egypt--</hi>as He lifted it up against Egypt at the Red Sea. <div eID="gen13858" type="x-p"/>
entries.c0124e599134987d04ae0574cd36990fe80a937f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8519"/><div sID="gen13859" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8519"/><hi type="bold">27. his burden--</hi>the Assyrians' oppression (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.3">Is 9:3</reference>). Judah was still tributary to Assyria; Hezekiah had not yet revolted, as he did in the beginning of Sennacherib's reign.<div eID="gen13859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13860" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because of--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.10.15">Ho 10:15</reference>).<div eID="gen13860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13861" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the anointing--</hi>namely, "Messiah" (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">Da 9:24</reference>). Just as in <reference osisRef="Isa.9.4-Isa.9.6">Is 9:4-6</reference>, the "breaking of the yoke of" the enemies' "burden and staff" is attributed to Messiah, "For unto us a child is born," &c., so it is here. Maurer not so well translates, "Because of the fatness"; an image of the Assyrians fierce and wanton pride drawn from a well-fed bull tossing off the yoke (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.15">De 32:15</reference>). So <reference osisRef="Isa.10.16">Is 10:16</reference> above, and <reference osisRef="Isa.5.17">Is 5:17</reference>, "fat ones." <div eID="gen13861" type="x-p"/>
entries.8ff1dc03e7ea34ee6aa3cbaf099f3fa1b172e833: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8520"/><div sID="gen13862" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8520"/>28-32. Onward gradual march of Sennacherib's army towards Jerusalem, and the panic of the inhabitants vividly pictured before the eyes.<div eID="gen13862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13863" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come to--</hi>come upon as a sudden invader (<reference osisRef="Gen.34.27">Ge 34:27</reference>).<div eID="gen13863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13864" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Aiath--</hi>same as Ai (<reference osisRef="Josh.7.2">Jos 7:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.7.32">Ne 7:32</reference>). In the north of Benjamin; so the other towns also; all on the line of march to Jerusalem.<div eID="gen13864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13865" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Michmash--</hi>nine miles northeast of Jerusalem.<div eID="gen13865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13866" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">laid up ... carriages--</hi>He has left his heavier baggage (so "carriages" for the things carried, <reference osisRef="Acts.21.15">Ac 21:15</reference>) at Michmash, so as to be more lightly equipped for the siege of Jerusalem. So <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.22">1Sa 17:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.13">25:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.24">30:24</reference> [Jerome and Maurer]. <div eID="gen13866" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb2c87fb05e2757c60a6fce5e0fdfe52b40d7cf4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8525"/><div sID="gen13879" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8525"/><hi type="bold">33. bough--</hi>literally, the "beauty" of the tree; "the beautiful branch."<div eID="gen13879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13880" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">high ones of stature--</hi>"the upright stem," as distinguished from the previous "boughs" [Horsley]. <div eID="gen13880" type="x-p"/>
entries.1c0a24bce2543967b80d93eb24b80bbdf804c580: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8526"/><div sID="gen13881" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8526"/>34. This verse and <reference osisRef="Isa.10.33">Is 10:33</reference> describe the sudden arrest and overthrow of Sennacherib in the height of his success; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.18">Is 10:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.19">19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.3">Eze 31:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.14">14</reference>, &c., contain the same image; "Lebanon" and its forest are the Assyrian army; the "iron" axe that fells the forest refers to the stroke which destroyed the one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.35">2Ki 19:35</reference>). The "Mighty One" is Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.21">Is 10:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>). <chapter eID="Isa.10"/>

entries.4dc60d9085b0a73c07a7380252e6bb1d6e84d759: <div eID="gen26955" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen26956" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26957" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26957" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26956" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26958" type="x-p"/> God's judgments against oppressive rulers, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.1-Isa.10.4">Isa 10:1-4</reference>. The prophet foretells the invasion of Sennacherib, and the destruction of his army. That mighty monarch is represented as a rod in the hand of God to correct his people for their sins; and his ambitious purposes, contrary to his own intentions, are made subservient to the great desires of Providence, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.5-Isa.10.11">Isa 10:5-11</reference>. Having accomplished this work, the Almighty takes account of his impious vauntings, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.12-Isa.10.14">Isa 10:12-14</reference>; and threatens utter destruction to the small and great of his army, represented by the thorns, and the glory of the forest, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.15-Isa.10.19">Isa 10:15-19</reference>. This leads the prophet to comfort his countrymen with the promise of the signal interposition of God in their favor, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.24-Isa.10.27">Isa 10:24-27</reference>. Brief description of the march of Sennacherib towards Jerusalem, and of the alarm and terror which he spread every where as he hastened forward, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.28-Isa.10.32">Isa 10:28-32</reference>. The spirit and rapidity of the description is admirably suited to the subject. The affrighted people are seen fleeing, and the eager invader pursuing; the cries of one city are heard by those of another; and groan swiftly succeeds to groan, till at length the rod is lifted over the last citadel. In this critical situation, however, the promise of a Divine interposition is seasonably renewed. The scene instantly changes; the uplifted arm of this mighty conqueror is at once arrested and laid low by the hand of heaven; the forest of Lebanon, (a figure by which the immense Assyrian host is elegantly pointed out, is hewn down by the axe of the Divine vengeance; and the mind is equally pleased with the equity of the judgment, and the beauty and majesty of the description, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.33">Isa 10:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.34">Isa 10:34</reference>.
entries.8f90363922e489bb19929a7e988d3c48f6d0e3df: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen26958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26959" type="x-p"/> My people - Instead of עמי ammi, my people, many MSS., and one of my own, ancient, read עמו ammo, his people. But this is manifestly a corruption.
entries.cc3a7fcdd8628b0ad076b1e4afa1ba1bd5b2785e: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen26959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26960" type="x-p"/> Without me - That is, without my aid: they shall be taken captive even by the captives, and shall be subdued even by the vanquished. "The י yod in בלתי bilti is a pronoun, as in <reference osisRef="Hos.13.4">Hos 13:4</reference>." - Kimchi on the place. One MS. has לבלתי lebilti. <div eID="gen26960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26961" type="x-p"/> As the people had hitherto lived without God in worship and obedience; so they should now be without his help, and should perish in their transgressions.
entries.908728635521c53fb8a064f858e1f0709e6af840: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen26961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26962" type="x-p"/> O Assyrian "Ho to the Assyrian" - Here begins a new and distinct prophecy, continued to the end of the twelfth chapter: and it appears from <reference osisRef="Isa.10.9-Isa.10.11">Isa 10:9-11</reference> of this chapter, that this prophecy was delivered after the taking of Samaria by Shalmaneser; which was in the sixth year of the reign of Hezekiah: and as the former part of it foretells the invasion of Sennacherib, and the destruction of his army, which makes the whole subject of this chapter it must have been delivered before the fourteenth of the same reign. <div eID="gen26962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26963" type="x-p"/> The staff in their hand "The staff in whose hand" - The word הוא hu, the staff itself, in this place seems to embarrass the sentence. I omit it on the authority of the Alexandrine copy of the Septuagint: nine MSS., (two ancient), and one of my own, ancient, for ומטה הוא umatter hu, read מטהו mattehu, his staff. Archbishop Secker was not satisfied with the present reading. He proposes another method of clearing up the sense, by reading ביום beyom, in the day, instead of בידם beyadam, in their hand: "And he is a staff in the day of mine indignation."
entries.f13002f11743e876ea241374c9e333d2ba68b259: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen26963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26964" type="x-p"/> The Lord "Jehovah" - For אדני Adonai, fourteen MSS. and three editions read יהוה Yehovah. <div eID="gen26964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26965" type="x-p"/> The fruit "The effect" - "פרי peri, f. צבי tsebi, vid. <reference osisRef="Isa.13.19">Isa 13:19</reference>, sed confer, <reference osisRef="Pro.1.31">Pro 1:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Pro.31.16">Pro 31:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Pro.31.31">Pro 31:31</reference>." - Secker. The Chaldee renders the word פרי peri by עיבדי obadey, works; which seems to be the true sense; and I have followed it. - L.
entries.bc729870374ef4b5f0d467d29ae05ba7f4253001: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen26965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26966" type="x-p"/> Like a valiant man "Strongly seated" - Twelve MSS. agree with the Keri in reading כביר kabbir, without the א aleph. And Sal. ben Melec and Kimchi thus explain it:" them who dwelled in a great and strong place I have brought down to the ground."
entries.c50ec816936451b9c57ef1e9052871d2d2af0682: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen26966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26967" type="x-p"/> No wood "Its master" - I have here given the meaning, without attempting to keep to the expression of the original, לא עץ lo ets, "the no-wood;" that which is not wood like itself, but of a quite different and superior nature. The Hebrews have a peculiar way of joining the negative particle לא lo to a noun, to signify in a strong manner a total negation of the thing expressed by the noun. "How hast thou given help (ללא כח lelo choach) to the no-strength? <div eID="gen26967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26968" type="x-p"/> And saved the arm (לא עז lo oz) of the no-power? <div eID="gen26968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26969" type="x-p"/> How hast, thou given counsel (ללא חכמה lelo chochmah) to the no-wisdom?" <reference osisRef="Job.26.2">Job 26:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.26.3">Job 26:3</reference>. <div eID="gen26969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26970" type="x-p"/> That is, to the man totally deprived of strength, power, and wisdom. "Ye that rejoice (ללא דבר lelo dabar) in nothing." <reference osisRef="Amo.6.13">Amo 6:13</reference>. <div eID="gen26970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26971" type="x-p"/> That is, in your fancied strength, which is none at all, a mere nonentity. "For I am God, (ולא איש velo ish), and no-man; <div eID="gen26971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26972" type="x-p"/> The Holy One in the midst of thee, yet do not frequent cities." <reference osisRef="Hos.11.9">Hos 11:9</reference>. "And the Assyrian shall fall by a sword (לא איש lo ish) of no-man; <div eID="gen26972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26973" type="x-p"/> And a sword of (לא אדם lo adam) no-mortal, shall devour him." <reference osisRef="Isa.31.8">Isa 31:8</reference>. "Wherefore do ye weigh out your silver (בלוא לחם belo lechem) for the no-bread." <reference osisRef="Isa.55.2">Isa 55:2</reference>. <div eID="gen26973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26974" type="x-p"/> So here לא עץ lo ets means him who is far from being an inert piece of wood, but is an animated and active being; not an instrument, but an agent.
entries.d60a2f2952efa71e7c3716cbaa64fb36fc502e7e: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen26974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26975" type="x-p"/> The Lord "Jehovah" - For אדני Adonai, fifty-two MSS., eleven editions, and two of my own, ancient, read יהוה, Yehovah, as in other cases. <div eID="gen26975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26976" type="x-p"/> And under his glory - That is, all that he could boast of as great and strong in his army, (Sal. ben Melec in loc.), expressed afterwards, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.18">Isa 10:18</reference>, by the glory of his forest, and of his fruitful field.
entries.fe9d1c79aa49134a4add589ea322e619daa69ea5: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen26976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26977" type="x-p"/> And it shall burn and devour his thorns "And he shall burn and consume his thorn" - The briers and thorns are the common people; the glory of his forest are the nobles and those of highest rank and importance. See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.9.17">Isa 9:17</reference>, and compare <reference osisRef="Eze.20.47">Eze 20:47</reference>. The fire of God's wrath shall destroy them, both great and small; it shall consume them from the soul to the flesh; a proverbial expression; soul and body, as we say; it shall consume them entirely and altogether; and the few that escape shall be looked upon as having escaped from the most imminent danger; "as a firebrand plucked out of the fire," <reference osisRef="Amo.4.11">Amo 4:11</reference>; ὡς δια πυρος, so as by fire, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.15">1Cor 3:15</reference>; as a man when a house is burning is forced to make his escape by running through the midst of the fire. <div eID="gen26977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26978" type="x-p"/> I follow here the reading of the Septuagint, כמאש נסס kemash noses, ὡς ὁ φευγων απω φλογος χαιομενης, as he who flees from the burning flame. Symmachus also renders the latter word by φευγων, flying.
entries.7a711e0258332101808484bd377d2758293b1783: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen26978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26979" type="x-p"/> The remnant shalt return - unto the mighty God - אל גבור El gibbor, the mighty or conquering God; the Messiah, the same person mentioned in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.6">Isa 10:6</reference> of the preceding chapter.
entries.1bacceaf85230800373cd434a37f480f4c15cc39: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen26979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26980" type="x-p"/> For though thy people Israel - I have endeavored to keep to the letter of the text as nearly as I can in this obscure passage; but it is remarkable that neither the Septuagint, nor St. Paul, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.28">Rom 9:28</reference>, who, except in a few words of no great importance, follows them nearly in this place, nor any one of the ancient Versions, take any notice of the word שטף shoteph, overflowing; which seems to give an idea not easily reconcilable with those with which it is here joined. 1. S. Maerlius (Schol. Philolog. ad Selecta S. Cod. loca) conjectures that the two last letters of this word are by mistake transposed, and that the true reading is שפט shophet, judging, with strict justice. The Septuagint might think this sufficiently expressed by εν δικαιοσυνῃ, in righteousness. One MS., with St. Paul and Septuagint Alex., omits בו bo in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.22">Isa 10:22</reference>; sixty-nine of Kennicott's and seventeen of De Rossi's MSS. and eight editions, omit כל col, all, in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.23">Isa 10:23</reference>; and so St. Paul, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.28">Rom 9:28</reference>. <div eID="gen26980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26981" type="x-p"/> The learned Dr. Bagot, dean of Christ Church, Oxford, afterwards Bishop of Bristol and Norwich, in some observations on this place, which he has been so kind as to communicate to me, and which will appear in their proper light when he himself shall give them to the public, renders the word כליון kilayon by accomplishment, and makes it refer to the predictions of Moses; the blessing and the curse which he laid before the people, both conditional, and depending on their future conduct. They had by their disobedience incurred those judgments which were now to be fully executed upon them. His translation is, The accomplishment determined overflows with justice; for it is accomplished, and that which is determined the Lord God of hosts doeth in the midst of the land. - L. Some think that the words might be paraphrased thus: The determined destruction of the Jews shall overflow with righteousness, (צדקה tsedakah), justification, the consequence of the Gospel of Christ being preached and believed on in the world. After the destruction of Jerusalem this word or doctrine of the Lord had free course, - did run, and was glorified.
entries.9d6dd0f92c2d0b5b047d6915e39932d4e4c90743: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen26981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26982" type="x-p"/> After the manner of Egypt "In the way of Egypt" - I think there is a designed ambiguity in these words. Sennacherib, soon after his return from his Egyptian expedition, which, I imagine, took him up three years, invested Jerusalem. He is represented by the prophet as lifting up his rod in his march from Egypt, and threatening the people of God, as Pharaoh and the Egyptians had done when they pursued them to the Red Sea. But God in his turn will lift up his rod over the sea, as he did at that time, in the way, or after the manner, of Egypt; and as Sennacherib has imitated the Egyptians in his threats, and came full of rage against them from the same quarter; so God will act over again the same part that he had taken formerly in Egypt, and overthrow their enemies in as signal a manner. It was all to be, both the attack and the deliverance, בדרך bederech, or כדרך kederech, as a MS. has it in each place, in the way, or after the manner, of Egypt.
entries.8328ab26dcd1ae2c218fd6eea3f048d48d46626c: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen26982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26983" type="x-p"/> The indignation "Mine indignation" - Indignatio mea, Vulg. ἡ οργη, Sept. μου η οργη κατα σου, MS. Pachom. Μου ἡ οργη ἡ κατα σου, MS. 1. D. 2. So that זעמי zaami, or הזעם hazzaam, as one MS. has it, seems to be the true reading.
entries.30554791cca6d7110b0260ac7d5445ef185016bd: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen26983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26984" type="x-p"/> And as his rod was upon the sea "And like his rod which he lifted up over the sea" - The Jewish interpreters suppose here an ellipsis of כ ke, the particle of similitude, before מטהו mattehu, to be supplied from the line above; so that here are two similitudes, one comparing the destruction of the Assyrians to the slaughter of the Midianites at the rock of Oreb; the other to that of the Egyptians at the Red Sea. Aben Ezra, Kimchi, Sal. ben Melec.
entries.d24f49a1c93999d739dca04d6527478af3085837: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen26984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26985" type="x-p"/> From off thy shoulder - Bishop Lowth translates the whole verse thus: - "And it shall come to pass in that day, <div eID="gen26985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26986" type="x-p"/> His burden shall be removed from off thy shoulder; <div eID="gen26986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26987" type="x-p"/> And his yoke off thy neck: <div eID="gen26987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26988" type="x-p"/> Yea, the yoke shall perish from off your shoulders.' <div eID="gen26988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26989" type="x-p"/> On which he gives us the following note: I follow here the Septuagint, who for מפני שמן mippeney shamen read משכמיכם mishshichmeychem, απο των ωμων ὑμων, from your shoulders, not being able to make any good sense out of the present reading. I will add here the marginal conjectures of Archbishop Secker, who appears, like all others, to have been at a loss for a probable interpretation of the text as it now stands." o. leg. שכם shakam; forte legend. מבני שמן mibbeney shamen, vide cap. <reference osisRef="Isa.5.1">Isa 5:1</reference>. <reference osisRef="Zac.4.14">Zac 4:14</reference> : Et possunt intelligi Judaei uncti Dei, <reference osisRef="Psa.105.15">Psa 105:15</reference>, vel Assyrii, משמנים mishmannim, hic <reference osisRef="Psa.105.16">Psa 105:16</reference>, ut dicat propheta depulsum iri jugum ab his impositum: sed hoc durius. Vel potest legi מפני שמי mippeney shami."
entries.7ee7fc5369094f7ef65dbe6aaa9ff497362a0f16: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen26989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26990" type="x-p"/> He is come to Aiath - A description of the march of Sennacherib's army approaching Jerusalem in order to invest it, and of the terror and confusion spreading and increasing through the several places as he advanced; expressed with great brevity, but finely diversified. The places here mentioned are all in the neighborhood of Jerusalem; from Ai northward, to Nob westward of it; from which last place he might probably have a prospect of Mount Sion. Anathoth was within three Roman miles of Jerusalem, according to Eusebius, Jerome and Josephus. Onomast. Loc. Hebr. et Antiq. Jud. 10:7, 3. Nob was probably still nearer. And it should seem from this passage of Isaiah that Sennacherib's army was destroyed near the latter of these places. In coming out of Egypt he might perhaps join the rest of his army at Ashdod, after the taking of that place, which happened about that time, (see <reference osisRef="Isa.20.1-Isa.20.6">Isa 20:1-6</reference>.); and march from thence near the coast by Lachish and Libnah, which lay in his way from south to north, and both which he invested till he came to the north-west of Jerusalem, crossing over to the north of it, perhaps by Joppa and Lydda; or still more north through the plain of Esdraelon.
entries.10fcf8231c526a3a197ed50b1ad82f5493aa080b: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen26990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26991" type="x-p"/> They are gone over the passage "They have passed the strait" - The strait here mentioned is that of Michmas, a very narrow passage between two sharp hills or rocks, (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.4">1Sam 14:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.5">1Sam 14:5</reference>), where a great army might have been opposed with advantage by a very inferior force. The author of the Book of Judith might perhaps mean this pass, at least among others: "Charging them to keep the passages of the hill country, for by them there was an entrance into Judea; and it was easy to stop them that would come up, because the passage was strait for two men at the most," Judith 4:7. The enemies having passed the strait without opposition, shows that all thoughts of making a stand in the open country were given up, and that their only resource was in the strength of the city. <div eID="gen26991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26992" type="x-p"/> Their lodging - The sense seems necessarily to require that we read למו lamo, to them, instead of לנו lanu, to us. These two words are in other places mistaken one for the other. <div eID="gen26992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26993" type="x-p"/> Thus <reference osisRef="Isa.44.7">Isa 44:7</reference>, for למו lamo, read לנו lanu, with the Chaldee; and in the same manner <reference osisRef="Psa.64.6">Psa 64:6</reference>, with the Syriac, and <reference osisRef="Psa.80.7">Psa 80:7</reference>, on the authority of the Septuagint and Syriac, besides the necessity of the sense.
entries.3d2cdd49f9972746d3f4769d8f7885d728af21de: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen26993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26994" type="x-p"/> Cause it to be heard unto Laish, O poor Anothoth "Hearken unto her, O Laish; answer her, O Anathoth!" - I follow in this the Syriac Version. The prophet plainly alludes to the name of the place, and with a peculiar propriety, if it had its name frown its remarkable echo. "ענתות anathoth, responsiones: eadem ratio nominis, quae in בית ענת beith anath, locus echus; nam hodienum ejus rudera ostenduntur in valle, scil. in medio montium, ut referent Robertus in Itiner. p. 70, et Monconnysius, p. 301." Simonis Onomasticon Vet. Test. - L. Anathoth - Answers, replies; for the same reason that Bethany, בית ענת berth anath, had its name, the house of echo; the remains of which are still shown in the valley, i.e., among the mountains.
entries.806360255e7d213a7fdbac6b681a5d690a1f7be6: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen26994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26995" type="x-p"/> Shall lop the bough with terror - פארה purah; but פורה purah, wine-press, is the reading of twenty-six of Kennicott's and twenty-three of De Rossi's MSS., four ancient editions, with Symmachus, Theodotion, and the Chaldee.
entries.098705487efecabfcee78dcf4daf9e72c7ac0763: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen26995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26996" type="x-p"/> Lebanon shall fall by a mighty one - באדיר beaddir, the angel of the Lord, who smote them, Kimchi. And so Vitringa understands it. Others translate, "The high cedars of Lebanon shall fall:" but the king of Assyria is the person who shall be overthrown.  <chapter eID="Isa.10"/> <div eID="gen26996" type="x-p"/>

entries.9d05d7af0cfff8b8c7d110e39b6e04fb2670b73c: <reference osisRef="Isa.10.1-Isa.10.4">Isa 10:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen12942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12943" type="x-p"/> Strophe 4. <hi type="italic">“Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees, and to the writers who prepare trouble to force away the needy from demanding justice, and to rob the suffering of my people of their rightful claims, that widows may become their prey, and they plunder orphans! And what will ye do in the day of visitation, and in the storm that cometh from afar? To whom will ye flee for help? and where will ye deposit your glory? There is nothing left but to bow down under prisoners, and they fall under the slain. With all this His anger is not turned away, but His hand is stretched out still.”</hi> This last strophe is directed against the unjust authorities and judges. The woe pronounced upon them is, as we have already frequently seen, Isaiah’s <hi type="italic">Ceterum censeo</hi>. <hi type="italic">Châkak</hi> is their decisive decree (not, however, in a denominative sense, but in the primary sense of hewing in, recording in official documents, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.8">Isa 30:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.19.23">Job 19:23</reference>); and <hi type="italic">Cittēb</hi> (<hi type="italic">piel</hi> only occurring here, and a perfect, according to Gesenius, §126, 3) their official signing and writing. Their decrees are <hi type="italic">Chikekē 'aven</hi> (an open plural, as in Jdg 5:15, for <hi type="italic">Chukkē</hi>, after the analogy of גללי, עממי, with an absolute <hi type="italic">Chăkâkim</hi> underlying it: Ewald, §186-7), inasmuch as their contents were worthlessness, i.e., the direct opposite of morality; and what they wrote out was <hi type="italic">‛âmâl</hi>, trouble, i.e., an unjust oppression of the people (compare πόνος and πονηρός).<note placement="foot">The current accentuation, ומכתבים <hi type="italic">mercha</hi>, עמל <hi type="italic">tiphchah</hi>, is wrong. The true accentuation would be the former with <hi type="italic">tiphchah</hi> (and <hi type="italic">metheg</hi>), the latter with <hi type="italic">mercha</hi>; for <hi type="italic">‛âmâl cittēbu</hi> is an attributive (an elliptical relative) clause. According to its etymon, <hi type="italic">‛âmâl</hi> seems to stand by the side of μῶλος, <hi type="italic">moles</hi>, <hi type="italic">molestus</hi> (see Pott in <hi type="italic">Kuhn’s Zeitschrift</hi>, ix. 202); but within the Semitic itself it stands by the side of אמל, to fade, <hi type="italic">marcescere</hi>, which coincides with the Sanscrit root <hi type="italic">mlâ</hi> and its cognates (see Leo Meyer, <hi type="italic">Vergleichende Grammatik</hi>, i. 353), so that <hi type="italic">‛âmâl</hi> is, strictly speaking, to wear out or tire out (vulg. to worry).</note> <div eID="gen12943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12944" type="x-p"/> Poor persons who wanted to commence legal proceedings were not even allowed to do so, and possessions to which widows and orphans had a well-founded claim were a welcome booty to them (for the diversion into the finite verb, see <reference osisRef="Isa.5.24">Isa 5:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.11">Isa 8:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.5">Isa 49:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.5">Isa 58:5</reference>). For all this they could not escape the judgment of God. This is announced to them in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.3">Isa 10:3</reference>, in the form of three distinct questions (commencing with <hi type="italic">ūmâh</hi>, <hi type="italic">quid igitur</hi>). The noun <hi type="italic">pekuddah</hi> in the <hi type="italic">first question</hi> always signifies simply a visitation of punishment; <hi type="italic">sho'âh</hi> is a confused, dull, desolate rumbling, hence confusion (<hi type="italic">turba</hi>), desolation: here it is described as “coming from afar,” because a distant nation (Asshur) was the instrument of God’s wrath. <hi type="italic">Second question:</hi> “Upon whom will ye throw yourselves in your search for help then” (<hi type="italic">nūs ‛al</hi>, a <hi type="italic">constr. praegnans</hi>, only met with here)? <hi type="italic">Third question:</hi> “Where, i.e., in whose hand, will ye deposit your wealth in money and possessions” (<hi type="italic">câbōd</hi>, what is weighty in value and imposing in appearance); <hi type="italic">‛âzab</hi> with <hi type="italic">b'yad</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.39.6">Gen 39:6</reference>), or with <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.39.14">Job 39:14</reference>), to leave anything with a person as property in trust. No one would relieve them of their wealth, and hold it as a deposit; it was irrecoverably lost. To this negative answer there is appended the following <hi type="italic">bilti</hi>, which, when used as a preposition after a previous negation, signifies <hi type="italic">praeter</hi>; when used as a conjunction, <hi type="italic">nisi</hi> (<hi type="italic">bilti 'im</hi>, Jdg 7:14); and where it governs the whole sentence, as in this case, <hi type="italic">nisi quod</hi> (cf., Num 11:6; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.18">Dan 11:18</reference>). In the present instance, where the previous negation is to be supplied in thought, it has the force of <hi type="italic">nil reliquum est nisi quod</hi> (there is nothing left but). The singular verb (<hi type="italic">câra‛</hi>) is used contemptuously, embracing all the high persons as one condensed mass; and tachath does not mean <hi type="italic">aeque ac</hi> or <hi type="italic">loco</hi> (like, or in the place of), as Ewald (§217, <hi type="italic">k</hi>) maintains, but is used in the primary and local sense of <hi type="italic">infra</hi> (below). Some crouch down to find room at the feet of the prisoners, who are crowded closely together in the prison; or if we suppose the prophet to have a scene of transportation in his mind, they sink down under the feet of the other prisoners, in their inability to bear such hardships, whilst the rest fall in war; and as the slaughter is of long duration, not only become corpses themselves, but are covered with corpses of the slain (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.14.19">Isa 14:19</reference>). And even with this the wrath of God is not satisfied. The prophet, however, does not follow out the terrible gradation any further. Moreover, the captivity, to which this fourth strophe points, actually formed the conclusion of a distinct period.
entries.6b6cff2bf16bddeafe6c340054aee373e9046e34: <reference osisRef="Isa.10.5-Isa.10.6">Isa 10:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen12944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12945" type="x-p"/> The law of contrast prevails in prophecy, as it does also in the history of salvation. When distress is at its height, it is suddenly brought to an end, and changed into relief; and when prophecy has become as black with darkness as in the previous section, it suddenly becomes as bright and cloudless as in that which is opening now. The <hi type="italic">hoi</hi> (woe) pronounced upon Israel becomes a <hi type="italic">hoi</hi> upon Asshur. Proud Asshur, with its confidence in its own strength, after having served for a time as the goad of Jehovah’s wrath, now falls a victim to that wrath itself. Its attack upon Jerusalem leads to its own overthrow; and on the ruins of the kingdom of the world there rises up the kingdom of the great and righteous Son of David, who rules in peace over His redeemed people, and the nations that rejoice in Him: - the counterpart of the redemption from Egypt, and one as rich in materials for songs of praise as the passage through the Red Sea. The Messianic prophecy, which turns its darker side towards unbelief in chapter 7, and whose promising aspect burst like a great light through the darkness in Isaiah 8:5-9:6, is standing now upon its third and highest stage. In chapter 7 it is like a star in the night; in Isaiah 8:5-9:6, like the morning dawn; and now the sky is perfectly cloudless, and it appears like the noonday sun. The prophet has now penetrated to the light fringe of <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1">Isa 6:1</reference>-13. The name <hi type="italic">Shear-yashub</hi>, having emptied itself of all the curse that it contained, is now transformed into a pure promise. And it becomes perfectly clear what the name Immanuel and the name given to Immanuel, <hi type="italic">El gibbor</hi> (mighty God), declared. The remnant of Israel turns to God the mighty One; and God the mighty is henceforth with His people in the Sprout of Jesse, who has the seven Spirits of God dwelling within Himself. So far as the date of composition is concerned, the majority of the more recent commentators agree in assigning it to the time of Hezekiah, because <reference osisRef="Isa.10.9-Isa.10.11">Isa 10:9-11</reference> presupposes the destruction of Samaria by Shalmanassar, which took place in the sixth year of Hezekiah. But it was only from the prophet’s point of view that this event was already past; it had not actually taken place. The prophet had already predicted that Samaria, and with Samaria the kingdom of Israel, would succumb to the Assyrians, and had even fixed the years (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.8">Isa 7:8</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.8.4">Isa 8:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.7">Isa 8:7</reference>). Why, then, should he not be able to presuppose it here as an event already past? The stamp on this section does not tally at all with that of Isaiah’s prophecy in the times of Hezekiah; whereas, on the other hand, it forms so integral a link in the prophetic cycle in chapters 7-12, and is interwoven in so many ways with that which precedes, and of which it forms both the continuation and crown, that we have no hesitation in assigning it, with Vitringa, Caspari, and Drechsler, to the first three years of the reign of Ahaz, though without deciding whether it preceded or followed the destruction of the two allies by Tiglath-pileser. It is by no means impossible that it may have preceded it. <div eID="gen12945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12946" type="x-p"/> The prophet commences with <hi type="italic">hoi</hi> (woe!), which is always used as an expression of wrathful indignation to introduce the proclamation of judgment upon the person named; although, as in the present instance, this may not always follow immediately (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.1.4">Isa 1:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.5-Isa.1.9">Isa 1:5-9</reference>), but may be preceded by the announcement of the sin by which the judgment had been provoked. In the first place, Asshur is more particularly indicated as the chosen instrument of divine judgment upon all Israel. <hi type="italic">“Woe to Asshur, the rod of mine anger, and it is a staff in their hand, mine indignation. Against a wicked nation will I send them, and against the people of my wrath give them a charge, to spoil spoil, and to prey prey, to make it trodden down like street-mire.”</hi> “<hi type="italic">Mine indignation</hi>:” <hi type="italic">za‛mi</hi> is either a permutation of the predicative הוּא, which is placed emphatically in the foreground (compare the אתּה־הּוּא in <reference osisRef="Jer.14.22">Jer 14:22</reference>, which is also written with <hi type="italic">makkeph</hi>), as we have translated it, though without taking הוּא as a copula (= <hi type="italic">est</hi>), as Ewald does; or else בידם הוּא is written elliptically for בידם הוּא אשׁר, “the staff which they hold is mine indignation” (Ges., Rosenmüller, and others), in which case, however, we should rather expect הוא זעמי בידם ומטה. It is quite inadmissible, however, to take <hi type="italic">za‛mi</hi> as a separate genitive to <hi type="italic">matteh</hi>, and to point the latter with <hi type="italic">zere</hi>, as Knobel has done; a thing altogether unparalleled in the Hebrew language.<note placement="foot">In the Arabic, such a separation does occur as a poetical licence (see De Sacy, <hi type="italic">Gramm</hi>. t. ii. §270).</note> <div eID="gen12946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12947" type="x-p"/> The futures in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.6">Isa 10:6</reference> are to be taken literally; for what Asshur did to Israel in the sixty year of Hezekiah’s reign, and to Judah in his fourteenth year, was still in the future at the time when Isaiah prophesied. Instead of וּלשׂימו the <hi type="italic">keri</hi> has וּלשׂוּמו, the form in which the infinitive is written in other passages when connected with suffixes (see, on the other hand, <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.7">2Sa 14:7</reference>). “<hi type="italic">Trodden down:</hi>” <hi type="italic">mirmas</hi> with short <hi type="italic">a</hi> is the older form, which was retained along with the other form with the a lengthened by the tone (Ewald §160,<hi type="italic">c</hi>).
entries.49232707e815a53599bb10300bbe450a7e9f61ee: <reference osisRef="Isa.10.7-Isa.10.11">Isa 10:7-11</reference> <div eID="gen12947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12948" type="x-p"/> Asshur was to be an instrument of divine wrath upon all Israel; but it would exalt itself, and make itself the end instead of the means. <reference osisRef="Isa.10.7">Isa 10:7</reference> <hi type="italic">“Nevertheless he meaneth not so, neither doth his heart think so; for it is in his heart to destroy and cut off nations not a few.”</hi> Asshur did not think so (<hi type="italic">lo'</hi>-<hi type="italic">cēn</hi>), i.e., not as he ought to think, seeing that his power over Israel was determined by Jehovah Himself. For what filled his heart was the endeavour, peculiar to the imperial power, to destroy not a few nations, i.e., as many nations as possible, for the purpose of extending his own dominions, and with the determination to tolerate no other independent nation, and the desire to deal with Judah as with all the rest. For Jehovah was nothing more in his esteem than one of the idols of the nations. <reference osisRef="Isa.10.8-Isa.10.11">Isa 10:8-11</reference> <hi type="italic">“For he saith, Are not my generals all kings? Is not Calno as Carchemish, or Hamath as Arpad, or Samaria as Damascus? As my hand hath reached the kingdoms of the idols, and their graven images were more than those of Jerusalem and Samaria; shall I not, as I have done unto Samaria and her idols, do likewise to Jerusalem and her idols?”</hi> The king of Asshur bore the title of the great king (<reference osisRef="Isa.36.4">Isa 36:4</reference>), and indeed, as we may infer from <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.7">Eze 26:7</reference>, that of the king of kings. The generals in his army he could call kings,<note placement="foot">The question is expressed in Hebrew phraseology, since <hi type="italic">sar</hi> in Assyrian was a superior title to that of <hi type="italic">melek</hi>, as we may see from inscriptions and proper names.</note> because the satraps<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Satrapes</hi> is the old Persian (arrow-headed) <hi type="italic">khshatra</hi> (Sanscr. <hi type="italic">xatra</hi>) <hi type="italic">pâvan</hi>, i.e., keeper of government. <hi type="italic">Pâvan</hi> (nom. <hi type="italic">pâvâ</hi>), which occurs in the <hi type="italic">Zendik</hi> as an independent word <hi type="italic">pavan</hi> (nom. <hi type="italic">pavao</hi>) in the sense of sentry or watchman, is probably the original of the Hebrew <hi type="italic">pechâh</hi> (see Spiegel, in Kohler on Mal 1:8).</note> who led their several contingents were equal to kings in the extent and splendour of their government, and some of them were really conquered kings (cf., 2Ki 25:28). He proudly asks whether every one of the cities named has not been as incapable as the rest, of offering a successful resistance to him. <hi type="italic">Carchemish</hi> is the later Circesium (Cercusium), at the junction of the Chaboras with the Euphrates (see above); <hi type="italic">Calno</hi>, the later <hi type="italic">Ctesiphon</hi>, on the left bank of the Tigris; <hi type="italic">Arpad</hi> (according to <hi type="italic">Merâshid</hi>, i. p. 47, in the pashalic of Chaleb, i.e., Aleppo) and <hi type="italic">Hamath</hi> (i.e., Epiphania) were Syrian cities, the latter on the river Orontes, still a large and wealthy place. The king of Asshur had also already conquered Samaria, at the time when the prophet introduced him as uttering these words. Jerusalem, therefore, would be unable to resist him. As he had obtained possession of idolatrous kingdoms (ל מעא, to reach, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.21.9">Psa 21:9</reference> : <hi type="italic">hâ</hi>-<hi type="italic">'elil</hi> with the article indicating the genus), which had more idols than Jerusalem or than Samaria; so would he also overcome Jerusalem, which had just as few and just as powerless idols as Samaria had. Observe there that <reference osisRef="Isa.10.11">Isa 10:11</reference> is the apodosis to <reference osisRef="Isa.10.10">Isa 10:10</reference>, and that the comparative clause of <reference osisRef="Isa.10.10">Isa 10:10</reference> is repeated in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.11">Isa 10:11</reference>, for the purpose of instituting a comparison, more especially with Samaria and Jerusalem. The king of Asshur calls the gods of the nations by the simple name of idols, though the prophet does not therefore make him speak from his own Israelitish standpoint. On the contrary, the great sin of the king of Asshur consisted in the manner in which he spoke. For since he recognised no other gods than his own Assyrian national deities, he placed Jehovah among the idols of the nations, and, what ought particularly to be observed, with the other idols, whose worship had been introduced into Samaria and Jerusalem. But in this very fact there was so far consolation for the worshippers of Jehovah, that such blasphemy of the one living God would not remain unavenged; whilst for the worshipers of idols it contained a painful lesson, since their gods really deserved nothing better than that contempt should be heaped upon them. The prophet has now described the sin of Asshur. It was ambitious self-exaltation above Jehovah, amounting even to blasphemy. And yet he was only the staff of Jehovah, who could make use of him as He would.
entries.75d7cc2a5cdf09ceadb16b9a1876c5edd202c8b1: <reference osisRef="Isa.10.12">Isa 10:12</reference> <div eID="gen12948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12949" type="x-p"/> And when He had made use of him as He would, He would throw him away. <hi type="italic">“And it will come to pass, when the Lord shall have brought to an end all His work upon Mount Zion and upon Jerusalem, I will come to punish over the fruit of the pride of heart of the king of Asshur, and over the haughty look of his eyes.”</hi> The “fruit” (<hi type="italic">peri</hi>) of the heart’s pride of Asshur is his vainglorious blasphemy of Jehovah, in which his whole nature is comprehended, as the inward nature of the tree is in the fruit which hangs above in the midst of the branches; <hi type="italic">tiph'ereth</hi>, as in Zec 12:7, the self-glorification which expresses itself in the lofty look of the eyes. Several constructives are here intentionally grouped together (Ges. §114, 1), to express the great swelling of Asshur even to bursting. But Jehovah, before whom humility is the soul of all virtue, would visit this pride with punishment, when He should have completely cut off His work, i.e., when He should have thoroughly completed (<hi type="italic">bizza'</hi>, <hi type="italic">absolvere</hi>) His punitive work upon Jerusalem (<hi type="italic">ma‛aseh</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.21">Isa 28:21</reference>). The prep. <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> is used in the same sense as in <reference osisRef="Jer.18.23">Jer 18:23</reference>, <hi type="italic">agere cum aliquo</hi>. It is evident that <hi type="italic">ma‛aseh</hi> is not used to indicate the work of punishment and grace together, so that <hi type="italic">yebazza‛</hi> could be taken as a literal future (as Schröring and Ewald suppose), but that it denotes the work of punishment especially; and consequently <hi type="italic">yebazza‛</hi> is to be taken as a <hi type="italic">futurum exactum</hi> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.4.4">Isa 4:4</reference>), as we may clearly see from the choice of this word in <reference osisRef="Lam.2.17">Lam 2:17</reference> (cf., Zec 4:9).
entries.83195e657542299446c8e0f3114d8e95690d5f43: <reference osisRef="Isa.10.13-Isa.10.14">Isa 10:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen12949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12950" type="x-p"/> When Jehovah had punished to such an extent that He could not go any further without destroying Israel - a result which would be opposed to His mercy and truth - His punishing would turn against the instrument of punishment, which would fall under the curse of all ungodly selfishness. <hi type="italic">“For he hath said, By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my own wisdom; for I am prudent: and I removed the bounds of the nations, and I plundered their stores, and threw down rulers</hi><note placement="foot">Thronende, lit., those who sat (on thrones).</note><hi type="italic">like a bull. And my hand extracted the wealth of the nations like a nest: and as men sweep up forsaken eggs, have I swept the whole earth; there was none that moved the wing, and opened the mouth, and chirped.”</hi> The futures may be taken most safely as regulated by the preterites, and used, like German imperfects, to express that which occurs not once merely, but several times. The second of these preterites, שׁושׂיתי, is the only example of a <hi type="italic">poel</hi> of verbs ל ה; possibly a mixed form from שׁסס (<hi type="italic">poel</hi> of שסס) and שהסה (<hi type="italic">piel</hi> of שסה). The object to this, viz., <hi type="italic">‛athidoth</hi> (<hi type="italic">chethib</hi>) or <hi type="italic">‛athudoth</hi> (<hi type="italic">keri</hi>), is sometimes used in the sense of τὰ μέλλοντα ; sometimes, as in this instance, in the sense of τὰ ὑπάρχοντα . According to the <hi type="italic">keri</hi>, the passage is to be rendered, “And I, a mighty one, threw down kings” (those sitting on thrones), <hi type="italic">cabbir</hi> being taken in the same sense as in <reference osisRef="Job.34.17">Job 34:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.34.24">Job 34:24</reference>; Job 36:5. But the <hi type="italic">chethib</hi> <hi type="italic">câ'abbı̄r</hi> is to be preferred as more significant, and not to be rendered “as a hero” (to which the <hi type="italic">Caph similitudinis</hi> is so little suitable, that it would be necessary to take it, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.13.6">Isa 13:6</reference>, as <hi type="italic">Caph veritatis</hi>), but “as a bull,” <hi type="italic">'abbı̄r</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.31">Psa 68:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.22.13">Psa 22:13</reference>; Psa 50:13. A bull, as the excavations show, was an emblem of royalty among the Assyrians. In <reference osisRef="Isa.10.14">Isa 10:14</reference>, the more stringent <hi type="italic">Vav conv.</hi> is introduced before the third pers. fem. The Kingdoms of the nations are compared here to birds’ nests, which the Assyrian took for himself (<hi type="italic">'âsaph</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Hab.2.5">Hab 2:5</reference>); and their possessions to single eggs. The mother bird was away, so that there was not even a sign of resistance; and in the nest itself not one of the young birds moved a wing to defend itself, or opened its beak to scare the intruder away. Seb. Schmid has interpreted to correctly, “<hi type="italic">nulla alam movet ad defendendum aut os aperit ad terrendum</hi>.” Thus proudly did Asshur look back upon its course of victory, and thus contemptuously did it look down upon the conquered kingdoms.
entries.6f982dfb6576906fc77aa0f931e033e8baccf56e: <reference osisRef="Isa.10.15">Isa 10:15</reference> <div eID="gen12950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12951" type="x-p"/> This self-exaltation was a foolish sin. <hi type="italic">“Dare the axe boast itself against him that heweth therewith, or the saw magnify itself against him that useth it? As if a staff were to swing those that lift it up, as if a stick should lift up not-wood!”</hi> “<hi type="italic">Not-wood</hi>” is to be taken as one word, as in Isa 31:8. A stick is wood, and nothing more; in itself it is an absolutely motionless thing. A man is “<hi type="italic">not-wood</hi>,” an incomparably higher, living being. As there must be “not-wood” to lay hold of wood, so, wherever a man performs extraordinary deeds, there is always a superhuman cause behind, viz., God Himself, who bears the same relation to the man as the man to the wood. The boasting of the Assyrian was like the bragging of an instrument, such as an axe, a saw, or a stick, against the person using it. The verb <hi type="italic">hēnı̄ph</hi> is applied both to saw and stick, indicating the oscillating movements of a measured and more or less obvious character. The plural, “those that lift it up,” points to the fact that by Him who lifts up the stock, Jehovah, the cause of all causes, and power of all powers, is intended.
entries.ad4c859ba8ef951a4c91cb66c78ba4c49c303bff: <reference osisRef="Isa.10.16">Isa 10:16</reference> <div eID="gen12951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12952" type="x-p"/> There follows in the next v. the punishment provoked by such self-deification (cf., <reference osisRef="Hab.1.11">Hab 1:11</reference>). <hi type="italic">“Therefore will the Lord, the Lord of hosts, send consumption against his fat men; and under Asshur’s glory there burns a brand like a firebrand.”</hi> Three epithets are here employed to designate God according to His unlimited, all-controlling omnipotence: viz., <hi type="italic">hâ'âdōn</hi>, which is always used by Isaiah in connection with judicial and penal manifestations of power; and <hi type="italic">adonâi</hi> <hi type="italic">zebâoth</hi>, a combination never met with again, similar to the one used in the Elohistic Psalms, <hi type="italic">Elohim zebaoth</hi> (compare, on the other hand, <reference osisRef="Isa.3.15">Isa 3:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.23-Isa.10.24">Isa 10:23-24</reference>). Even here a large number of codices and editions (Norzi’s, for example) have the reading <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> <hi type="italic">Zebaoth</hi>, which is customary in other cases.<note placement="foot">This passage is not included in the 134 <hi type="italic">vaddâ'ı̄n</hi> (i.e., “real”) <hi type="italic">adonai</hi>, or passages in which <hi type="italic">adonai</hi> is written, and not merely to be read, that are enumerated by the Masora (see <hi type="italic">Bär’s Psalterium</hi>, p. 133).</note><hi type="italic">Râzōn</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.17.4">Isa 17:4</reference>) is one of the diseases mentioned in the catalogue of curses in <reference osisRef="Lev.26.16">Lev 26:16</reference> and Deu 28:22. Galloping consumption comes like a destroying angel upon the great masses of flesh seen in the well-fed Assyrian magnates: <hi type="italic">mishmannim</hi> is used in a personal sense, as in Psa 78:31. And under the glory of Asshur, i.e., its richly equipped army (<hi type="italic">câbōd</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Isa.8.7">Isa 8:7</reference>), He who makes His angels flames of fire places fire so as to cause it to pass away in flames. In accordance with Isaiah’s masterly art of painting in tones, the whole passage is so expressed, that we can hear the crackling, and spluttering, and hissing of the fire, as it seizes upon everything within its reach. This fire, whatever it may be so far as its natural and phenomenal character is concerned, is in its true essence the wrath of Jehovah.
entries.4e16ef216b79525f9a71ee4d7b659d971d2f4b7b: <reference osisRef="Isa.10.17">Isa 10:17</reference> <hi type="italic">“And the light of Israel becomes a fire, and His Holy One a flame; and it sets on fire and devours its thistles and thorns on one day.”</hi> God is fire (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.3">Deu 9:3</reference>), and light (1Jo 1:5); and in His own self-life the former is resolved into the latter. <hi type="italic">Kâdōsh</hi> (holy) is here parallel to <hi type="italic">'ōr</hi> (light); for the fact that God is holy, and the fact that He is pure light, are essentially one and the same thing, whether <hi type="italic">kâdash</hi> meant originally to be pure or to be separate. The nature of all creatures, and of the whole <hi type="italic">cosmos</hi>, is a mixture of light and darkness. The nature of God alone is absolute light. But light is love. In this holy light of love He has given Himself up to Israel, and taken Israel to Himself. But He has also within Him a basis of fire, which sin excites against itself, and which was about to burst forth as a flaming fire of wrath against Asshur, on account of its sins against Him and His people. Before this fire of wrath, this destructive might of His penal righteousness, the splendid forces of Asshur were nothing but a mass of thistles and a bed of thorns (written here in the reverse order peculiar to Isaiah, <hi type="italic">shâmı̄r</hi> <hi type="italic">vâshaith</hi>), equally inflammable, and equally deserving to be burned. To all appearance, it was a forest and a park, but is was irrecoverably lost.
entries.0bfab34747d671eff7744c93c82d0d134cf943a5: <reference osisRef="Isa.10.18-Isa.10.19">Isa 10:18-19</reference> <hi type="italic">“And the glory of his forest and his garden-ground will He destroy, even to soul and flesh, so that it is as when a sick man dieth. And the remnant of the trees of his forest can be numbered, and a boy could write them.”</hi> The army of Asshur, composed as it was of many and various nations, was a forest (<hi type="italic">ya‛ar</hi>); and, boasting as it did of the beauty of both men and armour, a garden ground (<hi type="italic">carmel</hi>), a human forest and park. Hence the idea of “utterly” is expressed in the proverbial “even to soul and flesh,” which furnishes the occasion for a leap to the figure of the wasting away of a נסס (<hi type="italic">hap</hi>. <hi type="italic">leg</hi>. the consumptive man, from <hi type="italic">nâsas</hi>, related to <hi type="italic">nūsh</hi>, <hi type="italic">'ânash</hi>, Syr. <hi type="italic">n‛sı̄so</hi>, <hi type="italic">n‛shisho</hi>, a sick man, based upon the radical notion of melting away, cf., <hi type="italic">mâsas</hi>, or of reeling to and fro, cf., <hi type="italic">mūt</hi>, <hi type="italic">nūt</hi>, Arab. <hi type="italic">nâsa</hi>, <hi type="italic">nâta</hi>). Only a single vital spark would still glimmer in the gigantic and splendid colossus, and with this its life would threaten to become entirely extinct. Or, what is the same thing, only a few trees of the forest, such as could be easily numbered (<hi type="italic">mispâr</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Deut.33.6">Deu 33:6</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.21.17">Isa 21:17</reference>), would still remain, yea, so few, that a boy would be able to count and enter them. And this really came to pass. Only a small remnant of the army that marched against Jerusalem ever escaped. With this small remnant of an all-destroying power the prophet now contrasts the remnant of Israel, which is the seed of a new power that is about to arise.
entries.3d22b76795cd8e1cdb8ae10444530183d7353753: <reference osisRef="Isa.10.20">Isa 10:20</reference> <hi type="italic">“And it will come to pass in that day, the remnant of Israel, and that which has escaped of the house of Jacob, will not continue to stay itself upon its chastiser, and will stay itself upon Jehovah, the Holy One of Israel, in truth.”</hi> Behind the judgment upon Asshur there lies the restoration of Israel. “The chastiser” was the Assyrian. While relying upon this, Israel received strokes, because Jehovah made Israel’s staff into its rod. But henceforth it would sanctify the Holy One of Israel, putting its trust in Him and not in man, and that purely and truly (<hi type="italic">be'emeth</hi>, “in truth”), not with fickleness and hypocrisy. Then would be fulfilled the <hi type="italic">promise</hi> contained in the name Shear-yashub, after the fulfilment of the threat that it contained.
entries.60037873a8e8de47b74e40bab00eb65d336fb132: <reference osisRef="Isa.10.21">Isa 10:21</reference> <hi type="italic">“The remnant will turn, the remnant of Jacob, to God the mighty.”</hi> <hi type="italic">El gibbor</hi> is God as historically manifested in the heir of David (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Isa 9:6</reference>). Whilst Hosea (Hos 3:5) places side by side Jehovah and the second David, Isaiah sees them as one. In New Testament phraseology, it would be “to God in Christ.”
entries.8f941415c43d57fb58e95f27ed176261b9abe593: <reference osisRef="Isa.10.22-Isa.10.23">Isa 10:22-23</reference> <div eID="gen12952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12953" type="x-p"/> To Him the remnant of Israel would turn, but only the remnant. <hi type="italic">“For if thy people were even as the sea-sand, the remnant thereof will turn: destruction is firmly determined, flowing away righteousness. For the Lord, Jehovah of hosts, completes the finishing stroke and that which is firmly determined, within the whole land.”</hi> As the words are not preceded by any negative clause, <hi type="italic">ci 'im</hi> are not combined in the sense of <hi type="italic">sed</hi> or <hi type="italic">nisi</hi>; but they belong to two sentences, and signify <hi type="italic">nam si</hi> (for if). If the number of the Israelites were the highest that had been promised, only the remnant among them, or of them (<hi type="italic">bō</hi> partitive, like the French <hi type="italic">en</hi>), would turn, or, as the nearer definition <hi type="italic">ad Deum</hi> is wanting here, come back to their right position. With regard to the great mass, destruction was irrevocably determined (<hi type="italic">râchatz</hi>, τέμνειν, then to resolve upon anything, ἀποτόμως, 1Ki 20:40); and this destruction “overflowed with righteousness,” or rather “flowed on (<hi type="italic">shōtēph</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.18">Isa 28:18</reference>) righteousness,” i.e., brought forth righteousness as it flowed onwards, so that it was like a swell of the penal righteousness of God (<hi type="italic">shâtaph</hi>, with the accusative, according to Ges. §138, Anm. 2). That <hi type="italic">cillâyōn</hi> is not used here in the sense of completion any more than in <reference osisRef="Deut.28.65">Deu 28:65</reference>, is evident from <reference osisRef="Isa.10.23">Isa 10:23</reference>, where <hi type="italic">câlâh</hi> (fem. of <hi type="italic">câleh</hi>, that which vanishes, then the act of vanishing, the end) is used interchangeably with it, and <hi type="italic">necherâtzâh</hi> indicates judgment as a thing irrevocably decided (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.22">Isa 28:22</reference>, and borrowed from these passages in <reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Dan 9:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.36">Dan 11:36</reference>). Such a judgment of extermination the almighty Judge had determined to carry fully out (<hi type="italic">‛ōseh</hi> in the sense of a <hi type="italic">fut. instans</hi>) within all the land (<hi type="italic">b'kereb</hi>, within, not <hi type="italic">b'thok</hi>, in the midst of), that is to say, one that would embrace the whole land and all the people, and would destroy, if not every individual without exception, at any rate the great mass, except a very few.
entries.c7127dba1b86e29c109158b59c1e5d5649d6ef41: <reference osisRef="Isa.10.24">Isa 10:24</reference> <div eID="gen12953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12954" type="x-p"/> In these esoteric addresses, whoever, it is not the prophet’s intention to threaten and terrify, but to comfort and encourage. He therefore turns to that portion of the nation which needs and is susceptible of consolation, and draws this conclusion from the element of consolation contained in what has been already predicted, that they may be consoled. - <hi type="italic">“Therefore thus saith the Lord, Jehovah of hosts, My people that dwellest in Zion, be not afraid of Asshur, if it shall smite thee with the rod, and lift its stick against thee, in the manner of Egypt.”</hi> “Therefore:” <hi type="italic">lacēn</hi> never occurs in Hebrew in the sense of <hi type="italic">attamen</hi> (Gesenius and Hitzig), and this is not the meaning here, but <hi type="italic">propterea</hi>. The elevating appeal is founded upon what has just before been threatened in such terrible words, but at the same time contains an element of promise in the midst of the peremptory judgment. The very words in which the people are addressed, “My people that dwelleth on Zion,” are indirectly encouraging. Zion was the site of the gracious presence of God, and of that sovereignty which had been declared imperishable. Those who dwelt there, and were the people of God (the servants of God), not only according to their calling, but also according to their internal character, were also heirs of the promise; and therefore, even if the Egyptian bondage should be renewed in the Assyrian, they might be assured of this to their consolation, that the redemption of Egypt would also be renewed. “<hi type="italic">In the manner of Egypt:</hi>” <hi type="italic">b'derek Mitzraim</hi>, lit., in the way, i.e., the Egyptians’ mode of acting; <hi type="italic">derek</hi> denotes the course of active procedure, and also, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.26">Isa 10:26</reference> and <reference osisRef="Amos.4.10">Amo 4:10</reference>, the course of passive endurance.
entries.38028acebffc7a1991bc08ed5dbea937e74679ce: <reference osisRef="Isa.10.25-Isa.10.26">Isa 10:25-26</reference> <div eID="gen12954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12955" type="x-p"/> A still further reason is given for the elevating words, with a resumption of the grounds of consolation upon which they were founded. <hi type="italic">“For yet a very little the indignation is past, and my wrath turns to destroy them: and Jehovah of hosts moves the whip over it, as He smote Midian at the rock of Oreb; and His staff stretches out over the sea, and He lifts it up in the manner of Egypt.”</hi> The expression “a very little” (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.16.14">Isa 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.17">Isa 29:17</reference>) does not date from the actual present, when the Assyrian oppressions had not yet begun, but from the ideal present, when they were threatening Israel with destruction. The indignation of Jehovah would then suddenly come to an end (<hi type="italic">câlâh za‛am</hi>, borrowed in <reference osisRef="Dan.11.36">Dan 11:36</reference>, and to be interpreted in accordance with <reference osisRef="Isa.26.20">Isa 26:20</reference>); and the wrath of Jehovah would be, or go, <hi type="italic">‛al</hi>-<hi type="italic">tabilthâm</hi>. Luzzatto recommends the following emendation of the text, יתּם על־תּבל ואפּי, “and my wrath against the world will cease,” <hi type="italic">tēbēl</hi> being used, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.14.17">Isa 14:17</reference>, with reference to the <hi type="italic">oikoumenon</hi> as enslaved by the imperial power. But the received text gives a better train of thought, if we connect it with Isa 10:26. We must not be led astray, however, by the preposition <hi type="italic">‛al</hi>, and take the words as meaning, My wrath (burneth) over the destruction inflicted by Asshur upon the people of God, or the destruction endured by the latter. It is to the destruction of the Assyrians that the wrath of Jehovah is now directed; <hi type="italic">‛al</hi> being used, as it frequently is, to indicate the object upon which the eye is fixed, or to which the intention points (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.8">Psa 32:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.42">Psa 18:42</reference>). With this explanation <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.10.25">Isa 10:25</reference></hi> leads on to Isa 10:26. The destruction of Asshur is predicted there in two figures drawn from occurrences in the olden time. The almighty Judge would swing the whip over Asshur (<hi type="italic">‛orer</hi>, <hi type="italic">agitare</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.18">2Sa 23:18</reference>), and smite it, as Midian was once smitten. The rock of Oreb is the place where the Ephraimites slew the Midianitish king 'Oreb (Jdg 7:25). His staff would then be over the sea, i.e., would be stretched out, like the wonder-working staff of Moses, over the sea of affliction, into which the Assyrians had driven Israel (<hi type="italic">yâm</hi>, the sea, an emblem borrowed from the type; see Kohler on Zec 10:11, cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.66.6">Psa 66:6</reference>); and He would lift it up, commanding the waves of the sea, so that they would swallow Asshur. “In the manner of Egypt:” <hi type="italic">b'derek Mitzraim</hi> (according to Luzzatto in both instances, “on the way to Egypt,” which restricts the Assyrian bondage in a most unhistorical manner to the time of the Egyptian campaign) signifies in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.24">Isa 10:24</reference>, as the Egyptians lifted it up; but here, as it was lifted up above the Egyptians. The expression is intentionally conformed to that in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.24">Isa 10:24</reference> : because Asshur had lifted up the rod over Israel in the Egyptian manner, Jehovah would lift it up over Asshur in the Egyptian manner also.
entries.47bac155fbb8555635b9d212e1be85b50b9e3d6c: <reference osisRef="Isa.10.27">Isa 10:27</reference> <div eID="gen12955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12956" type="x-p"/> The yoke of the imperial power would then burst asunder. <hi type="italic">“And it will come to pass in that day, its burden will remove from thy shoulder, and its yoke from thy neck; and the yoke will be destroyed from the pressure of the fat.”</hi> We have here two figures: in the first (<hi type="italic">cessabit onus ejus a cervice tua</hi>) Israel is represented as a beast of burden; in the second (<hi type="italic">et jugum ejus a collo tuo</hi>), as a beast of draught. And this second figure is divided again into two fields. For <hi type="italic">yâsūr</hi> merely affirms that the yoke, like the burden, will be taken away from Israel; but <hi type="italic">chubbal</hi>, that the yoke itself will snap, from the pressure of his fat strong neck against it. Knobel, who alters the text, objects to this on the ground that the yoke was a cross piece of wood, and not a collar. And no doubt the simple yoke is a cross piece of wood, which is fastened to the forehead of the ox (generally of two oxen yoked together: <hi type="italic">jumenta</hi> = <hi type="italic">jugmenta</hi>, like <hi type="italic">jugum</hi>, from <hi type="italic">jungere</hi>); but the derivation of the name itself, <hi type="italic">‛ol</hi>, from <hi type="italic">‛âlal</hi>, points to the connection of the cross piece of wood with a collar, and here the yoke is expressly described as lying round the neck (and not merely fastened against the forehead). There is no necessity, therefore, to read <hi type="italic">chebel</hi> (<hi type="italic">chablo</hi>), as Knobel proposes; <hi type="italic">chubbal</hi> (Arabic <hi type="italic">chubbila</hi>) indicates her a <hi type="italic">corrumpi</hi> consequent upon a <hi type="italic">disrumpi</hi>. (On <hi type="italic">p'nē</hi>, vid., <reference osisRef="Job.41.5">Job 41:5</reference>; and for the application of the term <hi type="italic">mippenē</hi> to energy manifesting itself in its effects, compare <reference osisRef="Ps.68.3">Psa 68:3</reference> as an example.) Moreover, as Kimchi has observed, in most instances the yoke creates a wound in the fat flesh of the ox by pressure and friction; but here the very opposite occurs, and the fatness of the ox leads to the destruction of the yoke (compare the figure of grafting employed in <reference osisRef="Rom.11.17">Rom 11:17</reference>, to which Paul gives a turn altogether contrary to nature). Salvation, as the double turn in the second figure affirms, comes no less from within (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.10.27">Isa 10:27</reference></hi>) than from without (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.10.27">Isa 10:27</reference></hi>). It is no less a consequence of the world-conquering grace at work in Isaiah, than a miracle wrought for Israel upon their foes. <div eID="gen12956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12957" type="x-p"/> The prophet now proceeds to describe how the Assyrian army advances steadily towards Jerusalem, spreading terror on every hand, and how, when planted there like a towering forest, it falls to the ground before the irresistible might of Jehovah. Eichhorn and Hitzig pronounce this prophecy a <hi type="italic">vaticinium post eventum</hi>, because of its far too special character; but Knobel regards it as a prophecy, because no Assyrian king ever did take the course described; in other words, as a mere piece of imagination, as Ewald maintains. Now, no doubt the Assyrian army, when it marched against Jerusalem, came from the southwest, namely, from the road to Egypt, and not directly from the north. Sennacherib had conquered Lachish; he then encamped before Libnah, and it was thence that he advanced towards Jerusalem. But the prophet had no intention of giving a fragment out of the history of the war: all that he meant to do was to give a lively representation of the future fact, that after devastating the land of Judah, the Assyrian would attack Jerusalem. There is no necessity whatever to contend, as Drechsler does, against calling the description an ideal one. There is all the difference in the world between idea and imagination. Idea is the essential root of the real, and the reality is its historical form. This form, its essential manifestation, may be either this or that, so far as individual features are concerned, without any violation of its essential character. What the prophet here predicts has, when properly interpreted, been all literally fulfilled. The Assyrian did come from the north with the storm-steps of a conqueror, and the cities named were really exposed to the dangers and terrors of war. And this was what the prophet depicted, looking as he did from a divine eminence, and drawing from the heart of the divine counsels, and then painting the future with colours which were but the broken lights of those counsels as they existed in his own mind.
entries.12cb73de9b4be3a8857d87e41f2d30ae122d5f7f: <reference osisRef="Isa.10.28-Isa.10.34">Isa 10:28-34</reference> <div eID="gen12957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12958" type="x-p"/> Aesthetically considered, the description is one of the most magnificent that human poetry has ever produced. <hi type="italic">“He comes upon Ayyath, passes through Migron; in Michmash he leaves his baggage. They go through the pass: let Geba be our quarters for the night! Ramah trembles; Gibeah of Saul flees. Scream aloud, O daughter of Gallim! Only listen, O Laysha! Poor Anathoth! Madmenah hurries away; the inhabitants of Gebim rescue. He still halts in Nob today; swings his hand over the mountain of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem. Behold, the Lord, Jehovah of hosts, lops down the branches with terrific force; and those of towering growth are hewn down, and the lofty are humbled. And He fells the thickets of the forest with iron; and Lebanon, it falls by a Majestic One.”</hi> When the Assyrian came upon Ayyath (= <hi type="italic">Ayyah</hi>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.7.28">1Ch 7:28</reference> (?), <reference osisRef="Neh.11.31">Neh 11:31</reference>, generally <hi type="italic">hâ</hi>-<hi type="italic">‛ai</hi>, or <hi type="italic">'Ai</hi>), about thirty miles to the north-east of Jerusalem, he trod for the first time upon Benjaminitish territory, which was under the sway of Judaea. The name of this 'Ai, which signifies “stone-heap,” tallies, as Knobel observes, with the name of the <hi type="italic">Tell el-hagar</hi>, which is situated about three-quarters of an hour to the south-east of Beitîn, i.e., Bethel. But there are tombs, reservoirs, and ruins to be seen about an hour to the south-east of Beitin; and these Robinson associates with Ai. From Ai, however, the army will not proceed towards Jerusalem by the ordinary route, viz., the great north road (or “Nablus road”); but, in order to surprise Jerusalem, it takes a different route, in which it will have to cross three deep and difficult valleys. From Ai they pass to Migron, the name of which has apparently been preserved in the ruins of <hi type="italic">Burg Magrun</hi>, situated about eight minutes’ walk from Beitîn.<note placement="foot">I also find the name written <hi type="italic">Magrum</hi> (read <hi type="italic">Magrun</hi>), which is probably taken from a more correct hearsay than the <hi type="italic">Machrûn</hi> of Robinson (ii. 127).</note> <div eID="gen12958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12959" type="x-p"/> Michmash is still to be found in the form of a deserted village with ruins, under the name of <hi type="italic">Muchmâs</hi>, on the eastern side of the valley of Migron. Here they deposit their baggage (<hi type="italic">hiphkid</hi>, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.20">Jer 36:20</reference>), so far as they are able to dispense with it - either to leave it lying there, or to have it conveyed after them by an easier route. For they proceed thence through the pass of Michmash, a deep and precipitous ravine about forty-eight minutes in breadth, the present Wady Suweinit. “The pass” (<hi type="italic">ma‛bârâh</hi>) is the defile of Michmash, with two prominent rocky cliffs, where Jonathan had his adventure with the garrison of the Philistines. One of these cliffs was called <hi type="italic">Seneh</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.4">1Sa 14:4</reference>), a name which suggests <hi type="italic">es-Suweinit</hi>. Through this defile they pass, encouraging one another, as they proceed along the difficult march, by the prospect of passing the night in Geba, which is close at hand. It is still disputed whether this Geba is the same place as the following Gibeah of Saul or not. There is at the present time a village called Geba' below <hi type="italic">Muchmâs</hi>, situated upon an eminence. The almost universal opinion now is, that this is not Gibeah of Saul, but that the latter is to be seen in the prominent <hi type="italic">Tell</hi> (<hi type="italic">Tuleil</hi>) <hi type="italic">el-Fûl</hi>, which is situated farther south. This is possibly correct.<note placement="foot">This is supported by Robinson in his <hi type="italic">Later Biblical Researches in Palestine</hi> (1857), by Valentiner (pastor at Jerusalem), and by Keil in the <hi type="italic">Commentary on Joshua, Judges,</hi> etc. (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.21-Josh.18.28">Jos 18:21-28</reference>), where all the more recent writings on this topographical question are given.</note> <div eID="gen12959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12960" type="x-p"/> For there can be no doubt that this mountain, the name of which signifies “Bean-hill,” would be a very strong position, and one very suitable for Gibeah of Saul; and the supposition that there were two places in Benjamin named <hi type="italic">Geba</hi>, <hi type="italic">Gibeah</hi>, or <hi type="italic">Gibeath</hi>, is favoured at any rate by <reference osisRef="Josh.18.21-Josh.18.28">Jos 18:21-28</reference>, where <hi type="italic">Geba</hi> and <hi type="italic">Gibeath</hi> are distinguished from one another. And this mountain, which is situated to the south of <hi type="italic">er-Râm</hi> - that is to say, between the ancient Ramah and Anathoth - tallies very well with the route of the Assyrian as here described; whilst it is very improbable that Isaiah has designated the very same place first of all <hi type="italic">Geba</hi>, and then (for what reason no one can tell) Gibeah of Saul. We therefore adopt the view, that the Assyrian army took up its quarters for the night at Geba, which still bears this name, spreading terror in all directions, both east and west, and still more towards the south. Starting in the morning from the deep valley between Michmash and Geba, they pass on one side of Rama (the present <hi type="italic">er-Râm</hi>), situated half an hour to the west of Geba, which trembles as it sees them go by; and the inhabitants of Gibeath of Saul, upon the “Bean-hill,” a height that commands the whole of the surrounding country, take to flight when they pass by. Every halting-place on their route brings them nearer to Jerusalem. The prophet goes in spirit through it all. It is so objectively real to him, that it produces the utmost anxiety and pain.
