This is also the design of what he immediately adds —<div eID="gen42050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42051" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">To the mighty God;</hi> that is, to him whom the people, after having returned from their former apostasy, will acknowledge to be the guardian of their salvation. This attribute, <hi type="italic">mighty</hi>, is ascribed to God for the sake of the occasion on which the words were used. He might have thought it sufficient to have expressed <hi type="italic">power</hi> by the name <foreign xml:lang="he">אל</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">El</hi>,) <hi type="italic">God</hi>, which also signifies <hi type="italic">mighty</hi>; but he chose likewise to add to it <foreign xml:lang="he">גבור</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">gibbor</hi>,) that is, <hi type="italic">strong</hi> or <hi type="italic">mighty</hi>, in order to excite the people to greater confidence. How was it possible for the people to betake themselves to the Assyrians and Egyptians, but because they did not think that God was sufficient for them? This is the source of all evils, when we are not fully convinced that in God is everything that can be desired for our salvation.<div eID="gen42051" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.10.21" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42049" osisID="Isa.10.21" type="section"/>
entries.87f19c22866a16779e37fe3993603a867a796648: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.10.22" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.10.22" sID="gen42052" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42053" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">22.</hi> <hi type="italic">For though thy people be.</hi> He casts down hypocrites from foolish confidence; for they reckoned it enough to be the descendants of holy Abraham according to the flesh, and, therefore, on the sole ground of their birth, they wished to be accounted holy. Yet he exhorts the godly to patience, that they may learn to await calmly that calamity and diminution of their number, lest, when it took place, it should be unexpected, and give them uneasiness. He therefore comforts them, that they may not be grieved at so great desolation; for the Lord will at least collect <hi type="italic">a remnant</hi> of it.<div eID="gen42053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42054" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The consumption decreed.</hi> <foreign xml:lang="he">כלה</foreign> (<hi type="italic">chalah</hi>) means <hi type="italic">to finish</hi>, and it means also <hi type="italic">to consume</hi>. The latter is more appropriate. He calls this diminution of the people a <hi type="italic">consumption</hi>, and one that is <hi type="italic">completed</hi>; for he employs exaggerated language, the import of which is, that they were not far from utter extermination, there being very few that were saved.<div eID="gen42054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42055" type="x-p"/>The word <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> may be taken either in the genitive case, <hi type="italic">of</hi> <hi type="italic">Israel</hi>, or in the vocative case, <hi type="italic">O Israel</hi>, <note n="168"> <div sID="gen42056" type="x-p"/> That is, the passage may either be rendered, <hi type="italic">Though thy people</hi> <hi type="italic">of Israel be as the sand of the sea</hi>; or, <hi type="italic">Though thy</hi> <hi type="italic">people, O Israel, be as the sand of sea</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen42056" type="x-p"/> </note> so that in this way he addresses the patriarch Jacob, or all the godly under his name. But it is of little importance, for the meaning is the same, in whichsoever of these ways it be taken; and therefore it may be read in the genitive case, <hi type="italic">of Israel</hi>. Yet I am more inclined to view it as a proper name, to denote the true, and not the spurious Israelite. The bold address to the patriarch has a striking effect; for God, addressing a dead man, declares to the living that what he had formerly promised, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.13.16 Bible:Gen.22.17">Genesis 13:16, 22:17</reference>,) that the posterity of Abraham would be <hi type="italic">like</hi> <hi type="italic">the sand of the sea</hi>, did not apply to a promiscuous multitude, which had apostatized from godliness, but that there would be a kind of interruption in a corrupt nation, till shortly afterwards it should be renewed.<div eID="gen42055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42057" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Overflowing with righteousness, </hi>or<hi type="italic"> overflowing righteousness.</hi> <note n="169"> <div sID="gen42058" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Shall overflow with</hi> (Heb. <hi type="italic">in</hi>, or, <hi type="italic">among</hi>) <hi type="italic">righteousness</hi> — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42058" type="x-p"/> </note> Another consolation is added, that this very small company <hi type="italic">will overflow righteousness</hi>. When we see the Church distressed by such heavy calamities, that we think that it cannot be far from destruction, we are in danger of giving way to despondency, and of entertaining doubts about the mercy of God. Those whose minds are impressed with just views of the judgment of God, feel that this is the severest of all temptations. It was therefore necessary that godly minds should be fortified against it, that they might soothe their grief by pondering the benefit which would result from this calamity. The benefit was, that <hi type="italic">righteousness would overflow</hi> the whole world like a river; and he had formerly noticed this, when he said (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.10.20">Isaiah 10:20</reference>) that <hi type="italic">the remnant</hi> <hi type="italic">would trust in God in truth</hi><div eID="gen42057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42059" type="x-p"/>The word <hi type="italic">righteousness</hi> is explained in various ways. Some refer it to the preaching of the gospel, because by means of it, as Paul says,<div eID="gen42059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42060" type="x-p"/>the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.1.17">Romans 1:17</reference>;)<div eID="gen42060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42061" type="x-p"/>and by the agency of the Apostles, who were a small remnant of the Jews, it spread over the whole world. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.16.15">Mark 16:15</reference>.) Others choose rather to view it as meaning that that <hi type="italic">consumption</hi> was an evidence and proof of the <hi type="italic">righteousness</hi> of God in inflicting punishments so severe on his own people. But I prefer a more general exposition of it, namely, “This <hi type="italic">consumption</hi> will be sufficient to fill the whole world with <hi type="italic">righteousness</hi>. The <hi type="italic">remnant</hi> which shall survive it, though small, will be sufficient to cause such rivers of <hi type="italic">righteousness</hi> to flow, that the whole world shall be <hi type="italic">overflowed</hi> by them.”<div eID="gen42061" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.10.22" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42052" osisID="Isa.10.22" type="section"/>
entries.c00098416eb1f0ca112cab34a8ff4585f9f89a6d: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.10.23" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.10.23" sID="gen42062" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42063" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">23.</hi> <hi type="italic">For the Lord God of hosts shall make a consumption.</hi> This repetition again wounds the self-complacency of those who proudly despised God. It was almost incredible that the Jews, to whom so many promises had been given, and with whom God had made <hi type="italic">an everlasting</hi> <hi type="italic">covenant</hi>, should perish, as it were, in an instant; and it appeared to be even inconsistent with the unchangeable nature of God. The Prophet therefore declares that <hi type="italic">the Lord</hi> is the author of this <hi type="italic">consumption</hi>, in order to repress the pride of wicked men, who, relying on their present prosperity, thought that they were beyond all danger, and, swelling with that confidence, ridiculed all threats and warnings. “God,” says he, “will reduce your land to a desert, so that in the very midst it will be desolate, and will resemble a wilderness.”<div eID="gen42063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42064" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">In the midst of all the land.</hi> By <hi type="italic">the midst of the land</hi> he means its very heart, that is, its most fortified and best defended places. Some think that the word <foreign xml:lang="he">נהרצה</foreign> (<hi type="italic">neheratzah</hi>) is an adjective, <hi type="italic">determined</hi>; but for my part I view it as a substantive, <hi type="italic">consummation</hi>; <note n="170"> <div sID="gen42065" type="x-p"/> The Author’s version is, <hi type="italic">because a consumption and consummation</hi> <hi type="italic">will the Lord Jehovah of hosts make</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen42065" type="x-p"/> </note> and in this sense it is used by Daniel and in other passages. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Dan.9.27">Daniel 9:27</reference>.)<div eID="gen42064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42066" type="x-p"/>Paul quotes this passage, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.9.28">Romans 9:28</reference>,) but in somewhat different words from what the Prophet uses; for he follows the ordinary translation which at that time was generally used. Though Paul wrote correctly and faithfully, and in accordance with the Prophet’s real meaning, yet the words which he quotes from the Greek translation have led many to depart from what the Prophet actually meant. The Greek translator having used the word <foreign xml:lang="el">λόγος</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">logos</hi>,) that is, <hi type="italic">a discourse</hi>, many have entered into discussions about the Gospel, and have said that it denotes the repeal of the law, because it puts an end to ceremonies and figures, and therefore that it is a short and concise <hi type="italic">discourse</hi>, by which we are freed from the burden of the law under which the people groaned. But that has nothing to do with the Prophet’s meaning; for here he says that the <hi type="italic">consumption</hi> is a <hi type="italic">diminution</hi>, by which the people will be almost ruined. Paul’s design is not different, and the Greek translators meant nothing else; for by <foreign xml:lang="el">λόγος </foreign>(<hi type="italic">logos</hi>) they meant what is expressed by the Hebrew word <foreign xml:lang="he">דבר</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">dabar</hi>.) Though the Prophet does not make use of the word <foreign xml:lang="he">דבר</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">dabar</hi>,) yet the word which he uses means <hi type="italic">a thing consumed</hi>, that is, <hi type="italic">consumption</hi>, and the meaning of both words is the same. In short, Paul there repeats (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.9.28">Romans 9:28</reference>) what Isaiah had said in this passage about the future <hi type="italic">consumption</hi> of the people, and shows that this prediction was chiefly fulfilled in his own time, when the Jews were cut off from the kingdom of God on account of their ingratitude, and but <hi type="italic">a small remnant</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.1.9 Bible:Isa.10.22">Isaiah 1:9, 10:22</reference>) was preserved.<div eID="gen42066" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.10.23" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42062" osisID="Isa.10.23" type="section"/>
entries.67fdff7d409015424a4ca7d9627ccbd451cc6cea: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.10.24" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.10.24" sID="gen42067" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42068" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">24.</hi> <hi type="italic">Therefore, thus saith the Lord Jehovah of hosts.</hi> He goes on with the same consolation, which belongs to the godly alone, who at that time, undoubtedly, were few in number. A great number of persons gloried in the name of God, and wished to be accounted his people; but there were few who actually performed what they professed in words; and, therefore, he does not address all without reserve, but only those who needed consolation. The kingdom having been destroyed, they might entertain fears about themselves and their affairs, and might judge of their own condition from that of others, and therefore it was necessary to comfort them. This distinction ought to be observed, for otherwise it would be inconsistent to address to the same persons statements so different.<div eID="gen42068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42069" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And shall lift up his staff against thee in the way of Egypt</hi> <note n="171"> <div sID="gen42070" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">After the manner of Egypt</hi>. — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42070" type="x-p"/> </note> He adds a ground of consolation, namely, that that calamity will be nothing else than <hi type="italic">the lifting up of a rod</hi> to chastise, but not to destroy them. The preposition <foreign xml:lang="he">ב</foreign> (<hi type="italic">beth</hi>) denotes resemblance. <foreign xml:lang="he">דרך</foreign> (<hi type="italic">derech</hi>) means <hi type="italic">a pattern</hi>, and therefore I render it, <hi type="italic">after the pattern of Egypt</hi>. As if he had said, “Though the Assyrian be cruel, and in many ways aim at thy destruction, yet he shall only wound, he shall not slay thee.” He therefore mentioned the pattern of the Egyptian bondage, which was indeed very wretched, but yet was not deadly. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Exod.1.14 Bible:Exod.12.51">Exodus 1:14, 12:51</reference>.) It is customary with the Prophets, amidst perplexity or disorder, to remind the people to contemplate that deliverance by which God miraculously rescued them from the hands of Pharaoh, who was a most cruel tyrant. The meaning therefore is, “As the Lord was at that time victorious, and destroyed the Egyptians who had leagued for your destruction, so now he will quickly vanquish the Assyrians.”<div eID="gen42069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42071" type="x-p"/>Others render it, <hi type="italic">in the way of Egypt</hi>, because the Assyrians made war against the Jews on account of the Egyptians. But that exposition cannot be admitted; and if we carefully examine the matter, it will be found that there is none more appropriate than that which I have proposed, and which is also approved by the most learned commentators. There are two clauses which form a contrast; the oppression which the Egyptians laid upon them, and the calamity which should be inflicted soon afterwards by the Assyrians. “As the oppression of the Egyptians was not deadly, so neither will the oppression of the Assyrians be. You have had experience of my strength and power against Pharaoh, and so will you find it on Sennacherib.” If we did not explain the clauses in this way, they would not agree with each other.<div eID="gen42071" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.10.24" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42067" osisID="Isa.10.24" type="section"/>
entries.bc930b54911e35d5dd3be150707ff3179d5e5032: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.10.25" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.10.25" sID="gen42072" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42073" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">25.</hi> <hi type="italic">But yet a little while.</hi> He means not only the siege of Jerusalem, when Sennacherib surrounded it with a numerous army, (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.17">2 Kings 18:17</reference>,) but likewise the rest of the calamities, when Jerusalem was overthrown, (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.25.4">2 Kings 25:4</reference>,) the Temple razed, and the inhabitants taken prisoners; for against those dreadful calamities it was necessary that the godly should be fortified by these promises. This ought to be carefully observed; for if we neglect it, as other commentators do, we shall not be able to see how the statements agree. Accordingly, the captivity of the people might be called a <hi type="italic">consumption</hi>; for Babylon was like a grave, and banishment was like death. But when the danger was immediate and urgent, and Sennacherib attacked them with his army, and various straits were felt by them in that siege, this consolation was needful; for Judea seemed to be utterly ruined, and to outward appearance no hope of safety was left.<div eID="gen42073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42074" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">My fury and indignation shall be spent.</hi> <note n="172"> <div sID="gen42075" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">The indignation shall cease, and mine anger</hi>. — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42075" type="x-p"/> </note> The consolation corresponds to this state of things. “The Lord will spare thee. For a time, indeed, he will delay, and will keep his assistance as it were concealed; but he will at length rescue thee, and will revenge thy enemies whom he has determined utterly to destroy.” If it be thought better to interpret <foreign xml:lang="he">כלה</foreign> (<hi type="italic">chalah</hi>) as meaning to <hi type="italic">consume</hi> or <hi type="italic">spend</hi>, then he says that <hi type="italic">he spends his anger</hi>, in the same way that we speak of <hi type="italic">spending</hi> years and our whole life; that is, “I will cherish my anger until I completely destroy the Assyrians.” But the word <hi type="italic">finish</hi> brings out the meaning more fully; as if he had said, “until I have discharged all my anger.” This is the destruction which he also threatens elsewhere (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.52.1">Isaiah 52:1</reference>) to the <hi type="italic">uncircumcised</hi>; for when the hope of mercy has been taken away, he executes his judgment against the ungodly.<div eID="gen42074" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.10.25" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42072" osisID="Isa.10.25" type="section"/>
entries.a91dbbaaa33c6fc71392bb65c34205069a7a85f3: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.10.26" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.10.26" sID="gen42076" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42077" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">26.</hi> <hi type="italic">And the LORD of hosts will stir up a scourge for him.</hi> Here Isaiah makes use of the word <hi type="italic">scourge</hi>, and not <hi type="italic">rod</hi>, meaning that the Lord will treat the enemies much more harshly and severely than they had treated the Jews. He threatens them with extermination, and makes it more evident by two examples; first, that of the Midianites, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Judg.7.25">Judges 7:25</reference>,) who were cut off by a dreadful slaughter in the valley of <hi type="italic">Oreb</hi>, which was so named from their leader, and, secondly, that of the Egyptians, whom the Lord, when they pursued after his people, sank in the Red Sea. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Exod.14.27 Bible:Exod.14.28">Exodus 14:27, 28</reference>.) In the former passage, he refers to a narrative which was somewhat more recent, and in the latter to one that was more ancient.<div eID="gen42077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42078" type="x-p"/>Hence we infer that the Lord hath displayed his power in defending his Church, in order that, when our affairs are in the most desperate state, we may remain steadfastly in the faith, and, relying on his grace, we still may cherish a pleasing hope. By means and in ways that are unexpected he often delivers his Church, as he did by the hands of Gideon and Moses. We ought always, therefore, to call to remembrance those benefits, that we may be excited more and more to confidence and perseverance.<div eID="gen42078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42079" type="x-p"/>Hence we ought also to infer that all the afflictions which we endure are the Lord’s rods with which he chastises us; and yet he does not permit Satan or his agents to inflict deadly chastisements upon us. On the other hand, an awful destruction awaits our enemies, as we see in the Midianites and Egyptians. It is therefore no small consolation that, when we compare our condition with theirs, we see them, for a time indeed, in all the madness of joy and of wickedness insulting the children of God, but at the same time learn what a dreadful sentence has been pronounced against them; for they are devoted to deadly and everlasting destruction.<div eID="gen42079" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.10.26" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42076" osisID="Isa.10.26" type="section"/>
entries.0fa726409a7de23471a93c6ce1c8c4dc4ffeaf27: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.10.27" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.10.27" sID="gen42080" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42081" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">27. </hi><hi type="italic">And it shall come to pass in that day.</hi> It is uncertain whether he now speaks of the deliverance which took place under Zerubbabel, (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Chr.36.22 Bible:2Chr.36.23">2 Chronicles 36:22, 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Ezra.1.2">Ezra 1:2</reference>,) or of that wonderful overthrow of Sennacherib, (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.19.35">2 Kings 19:35</reference>,) when he besieged Jerusalem with a huge army. This latter opinion is almost universally preferred; and indeed it appears to be supported by what follows, for immediately afterwards he gives a description of the country, and enumerates the chief places through which Sennacherib should conduct his army, till he arrived at Jerusalem itself, so that there appeared to be nothing at all to hinder him from taking possession of the city. With this opinion I partly agree, but I extend the prediction farther.<div eID="gen42081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42082" type="x-p"/>Isaiah intends to comfort the godly who were involved in the present distress. It might be thought that the promise failed, and that the calamities which immediately followed were utterly at variance with it. For instance, if the Lord promise to give me food for next year, and yet leave me altogether destitute of it, what faith can I have in a promise so distant, if the Lord do not rescue me from the present distress? Thus, the Lord’s promise, in which he had said that he would deliver his people from Babylon, and would continually assist them, may be thought to have failed, when it was exposed to the jaws of that huge wild beast. With the view of meeting this objection, the Prophet includes both promises, that the Lord will be the guardian of his people, till at length he deliver them from death. Some limit it to the slaughter (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.19.35">2 Kings 19:35</reference>) of Sennacherib’s army; but as Isaiah promises <hi type="italic">the</hi> <hi type="italic">loosing</hi>, or <hi type="italic">breaking of the yoke</hi>, I have no doubt that he describes deliverance from captivity. Yet he confirms the promise, that God will not only rescue them from Babylon, but will also aid them against the besieging army of the tyrant, whom he will not suffer to go beyond what has been threatened.<div eID="gen42082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42083" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">That his burden shall be taken away from off thy shoulder, and his yoke from off thy neck,</hi> He describes that tyranny in two ways, in order to illustrate more fully how great was the blessing of deliverance. If it be thought best to refer it to Sennacherib, he had not laid on the Jews so grievous a yoke. The people paid only some tribute, as we learn from sacred history. (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.23.33">2 Kings 23:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:2Chr.36.3">2 Chronicles 36:3</reference>.) Why then has he employed two names in describing this tyranny? It may be pleaded that he had in his eye the approaching danger; for that tyrant, like a huge beast of prey, had devoured the whole of Judea by his voraciousness, and had oppressed them to such an extent, that it appeared to be almost impossible that his <hi type="italic">yoke</hi> could ever be taken off. But I have already explained the view which I prefer, that he describes the uninterrupted course of the favor of God down to the time of redemption.<div eID="gen42083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42084" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And the yoke shall be destroyed from the face of the anointing.</hi> <note n="173"> <div sID="gen42085" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Because of the anointing</hi>. — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42085" type="x-p"/> </note> The phrase, <hi type="italic">the face of the anointing</hi>, is explained by some to mean the <hi type="italic">fatness</hi> with which <hi type="italic">the yoke</hi> is besmeared. But that interpretation is too farfetched. Others more correctly view <foreign xml:lang="he">שמן</foreign> (<hi type="italic">shamen</hi>) as bearing its ordinary signification, and as denoting <hi type="italic">anointing</hi> or <hi type="italic">oil</hi>. He again reminds them of Christ, and shows that through his kindness they will be delivered from that tyranny. <hi type="italic">Anointing</hi> is the name given to that kingdom which the Lord had set apart for himself, and which he therefore wished to keep unspotted and undiminished. When the Prophets intend to applaud the majesty of that kingdom, they speak of the <hi type="italic">anointing</hi> which the Lord had bestowed on it as a distinguishing mark, because it was a type of Christ. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.45.7 Bible:Ps.89.20 Bible:Isa.61.1 Bible:Dan.9.24">Psalm 45:7, 89:20; Isaiah 61:1; Daniel 9:24</reference>.) Though God established the rest of the kingdoms, still they were in some respects profane; this ranked above them as holy and sacred, because the Lord reigned over Judea in a peculiar manner, and because under this figure of a kingdom he held up Christ to their view. For this reason, also, it was promised to Solomon that his throne would be everlasting. (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Sam.7.13 Bible:1Chr.22.10 Bible:Ps.89.5">2 Samuel 7:13; ; </reference><reference osisRef="Bible:1Chr.22.10">1 Chronicles 22:10</reference><reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.89.5">Psalm 89:5</reference>.) As to the interpretation given by some, that <foreign xml:lang="he">שמן</foreign> (<hi type="italic">shamen</hi>) denotes the king himself, not only is it too farfetched, but it conveys no solid instruction.<div eID="gen42084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42086" type="x-p"/>The Prophet therefore points out the means of overthrowing that tyranny; for it appeared as if there were no reason to believe that the yoke of so powerful a tyrant would be broken. He shows that this will arise from the heavenly anointing of that kingdom, that all may perceive that this benefit depends on the power of Christ, and not on the ability of man or on chance.<div eID="gen42086" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.10.27" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42080" osisID="Isa.10.27" type="section"/>
entries.653702d9bd68cbd78f240d12b0fe628d00e1b39e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.10.28" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.10.28" sID="gen42087" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42088" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">28.</hi> <hi type="italic">He is come to Aiath.</hi> The siege of the holy city being now at hand, Isaiah sets before their eyes the whole of Sennacherib’s march, that the hearts of the godly, by long and careful study of it, may remain steadfast. This delineation was powerfully calculated to allay their fears, when godly men saw that the Assyrians did not move a step but by the appointment of God; for by the mouth of the Prophet he had given a lively description of the whole of that march. <note n="174"> <div sID="gen42089" type="x-p"/> “Here is a lively description of the march of Sennacherib’s army, not that related below in <reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.36.1-Isa.36.22">chapter 36:1-22</reference>, but in his first invasion of Judea, when he passed Jerusalem to the northward on his way to Egypt; for so the places here mentioned indicate, stretching in order from the north to the west and south of that capital.” — <hi type="italic">Rosenmuller</hi>.<div eID="gen42089" type="x-p"/> </note> It is unnecessary to spend much time in explaining the relative position of the places here named, for it is enough if we understand that Sennacherib marched through those places of which the Jews had been informed.<div eID="gen42088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42090" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">At Michmash he will lay up his baggage</hi>. The words which we render, <hi type="italic">He will lay up his baggage</hi> or <hi type="italic">armor</hi>, are translated by some, <hi type="italic">He hath made a muster</hi>; for <foreign xml:lang="he">פקד</foreign> (<hi type="italic">pakad</hi>) signifies also to <hi type="italic">number</hi>. I do not dislike this interpretation, but prefer the former; for I understand the Prophet to mean that the Assyrian <hi type="italic">will lay up his armor</hi>, that is, the provisions, and the rest of the implements of war, <hi type="italic">in Michmash</hi>. It is the custom of warriors not to lead forward an army without providing the means of support, which they <hi type="italic">lay up</hi> in a safe and convenient place, that the army may be supplied out of it with all that is needful. Under the word <hi type="italic">baggage</hi> or <hi type="italic">arms</hi>, he includes not only <hi type="italic">darts</hi> and <hi type="italic">swords</hi>, but all the supplies and provisions of war. The meaning of the word <foreign xml:lang="he">כלי</foreign> (<hi type="italic">cheli</hi>) is extensive, and includes every kind of implements, and thus resembles the word (<foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">vasa</hi></foreign>) which denotes <hi type="italic">vessels</hi> in the Latin language.<div eID="gen42090" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.10.28" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42087" osisID="Isa.10.28" type="section"/>
entries.d87c0e546108facadbc90f85103fff05360820ec: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.10.29" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.10.29" sID="gen42091" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42092" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">29.</hi><hi type="italic"> They have crossed the ford.</hi> <note n="175"> <div sID="gen42093" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">They are gone over the passage</hi>. — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42093" type="x-p"/> </note> Some understand by this the passage of the Jordan, but I do not know if it could be <hi type="italic">crossed</hi> by a <hi type="italic">ford</hi> in that quarter. <note n="176"> <div sID="gen42094" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">They have passed the strait</hi>. The strait here mentioned is that of Michmas, a very narrow passage between two sharp hills or rocks, (see <reference osisRef="Bible:1Sam.14.4 Bible:1Sam.14.5">1 Samuel 14:4, 5</reference>,) where a great army might have been opposed with advantage by a very inferior force. The enemies having <hi type="italic">passed the strait</hi> without opposition, shows that all thoughts of making a stand in the open country were given up, and that their only resource was in the strength of the city.” — <hi type="italic">Lowth</hi>.<div eID="gen42094" type="x-p"/> </note> He describes how great will be the terror when they hear of the approach of the Assyrian, that the whole country will be struck with terror and alarm, so that the Assyrian will subdue it without any difficulty. When such dread has seized their hearts, they will freely surrender at the first attack of the enemy, so that the conquerors will be allowed to ravage at their pleasure. He passes from the singular to the plural number, because he speaks sometimes of the king and sometimes of the whole army.<div eID="gen42092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42095" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Ramah is afraid; Gibeah of Saul is fled.</hi> He mentions <hi type="italic">Ramah</hi> in preference to the rest, because it was the nearest town; and he describes the flight of the inhabitants of some towns, as if the mere report had terrified them to such a degree that they gave up their country into the enemy’s hand. After having spoken of so great dismay, he adds. —<div eID="gen42095" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.10.29" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42091" osisID="Isa.10.29" type="section"/>

(Heb. <hi type="italic">Cry shrill with thy voice</hi>.) — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42098" type="x-p"/> </note> <hi type="italic"> O daughter of Gallim.</hi> By the word <hi type="italic">neigh</hi> he denotes the howling and cries which will be heard at a distance. It is very common, in the Hebrew language, to call cities <hi type="italic">daughters</hi>. He says that the howling will be so great that it will be heard even by the neighboring cities; for at <hi type="italic">Laish</hi> will be heard the groanings which will be uttered in <hi type="italic">Anathoth</hi><div eID="gen42097" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.10.30" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42096" osisID="Isa.10.30" type="section"/>
entries.d17b9cc39bd0c7f027ea2a1a9d8416483cd78559: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.10.31" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.10.31" sID="gen42099" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42100" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">31.</hi> <hi type="italic">Madmenah is removed.</hi> In exaggerated language he describes that city to have been shaken to such a degree, as if it had been <hi type="italic">removed</hi> to another place. This relates to the disorderly movements of a people in flight; as if he had said that the inhabitants of that city were thrown into as great a commotion as if the city had been razed to its foundations.<div eID="gen42100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42101" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The inhabitants of Gebim have gathered themselves.</hi> This may be explained to mean that they are so terrified that they crowd together in a body. Others understand by it, that they rush out in a disorderly manner, as if there were not room for a free passage.<div eID="gen42101" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.10.31" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42099" osisID="Isa.10.31" type="section"/>
entries.0541219558047ee17cb507d45b6b8102cd2ce007: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.10.32" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.10.32" sID="gen42102" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42103" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">32.</hi> <hi type="italic">Yet a day.</hi> <note n="178"> <div sID="gen42104" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Yet this day</hi>. One day longer shall the Assyrian be permitted to remain in the vicinity of <hi type="italic">Jerusalem</hi>, and to affright <hi type="italic">the</hi> <hi type="italic">daughter of Zion</hi>.” — <hi type="italic">Stock</hi>.<div eID="gen42104" type="x-p"/> </note> Some interpret this, that the Assyrian will yet remain <hi type="italic">one day in Nob</hi>, which was a village contiguous to Jerusalem, as Jerome and others declare. But I rather agree with those who think that it means, that he will have a great part of the day before him when he halts there, in order to make preparations for besieging Jerusalem on the following day. He intends to describe the rapid march of the Assyrian, and how near Jerusalem was to utter destruction; as if he had said, that he had but a small part of the journey to perform, and that before <hi type="italic">the day</hi> was ended, he would arrive at that city.<div eID="gen42103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42105" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">He shall shake the hand.</hi> This contributes still more to show their terror; for Sennacherib, having conquered the whole country, will threaten Jerusalem, as if he could storm it by the slightest expression of his will.<div eID="gen42105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42106" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Against the mountain of the daughter of Zion.</hi> By a figure of speech, in which a part is taken for the whole, (<foreign xml:lang="el">συνεκδοχικῶς</foreign>,) he includes the whole city under the name of <hi type="italic">the mountain</hi>, because that part was higher, and commanded a view of the other quarters of the city. From this confidence of the tyrant, he shows that Jerusalem was not far from utter destruction; for the whole country, and even the city, was struck with such terror that none ventured to oppose him. By these details, therefore, the Prophet intended to give a more impressive view of the kindness of God, that it ought to be ascribed to the extraordinary favor and goodness of God, and not to human aid, of which there was none, that Jerusalem was preserved, as if a sheep had been rescued from the jaws of a lion.<div eID="gen42106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42107" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Behold, the Lord Jehovah of hosts.</hi> Almost all explain this passage as referring to the Assyrians. (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.19.35">2 Kings 19:35</reference>.) They think that the Prophet threatens against them that slaughter with which the Lord destroyed them, after that they had besieged Jerusalem. As if he had spoken in this manner: The Assyrian will indeed be elated with such pride, that as soon as he has seen Jerusalem, he will think that it is in his power. All being struck with such dismay at his approach, that some shall flee and others shall freely surrender themselves, he will imagine that all are subdued under him; but the Lord will quickly reverse his condition, and <hi type="italic">lop off those lofty branches</hi><div eID="gen42107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42108" type="x-p"/>But for my own part, when I examine closely the whole passage, and especially what he adds soon afterwards about <hi type="italic">Lebanon</hi>, and the consolation which immediately follows, I think that this passage ought to be referred to the Jews themselves. Isaiah therefore proceeds, in my opinion, to threaten the calamities which awaited the people. As if he had said, “Not only will he come to <hi type="italic">Nob</hi>, but he will spread devastation far and wide over the whole country. Everything in it that is excellent and lofty, he will completely waste and destroy, in the same manner as if one should cut off branches from a tree or cut down a tree from the root.”<div eID="gen42108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42109" type="x-p"/>This interpretation is confirmed by the following chapter, in which the Prophet offers consolation against that calamity; for the consolation agrees with this verse, and is added as an appropriate remedy for soothing grief. Nor do I attach any importance to the division of the chapter, which is often very absurd, and which perplexes the whole of the Prophet’s meaning. I think, therefore, that we ought to connect that consolation with these verses, as if there had been no such division.<div eID="gen42109" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.10.32" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42102" osisID="Isa.10.32" type="section"/>

34. And he will cut down the thick places of the forest with iron. There is no difficulty in explaining this metaphor, for it is plain enough that by tall and high trees is denoted all that is powerful, excellent, or lofty. Thus he foretells the destruction and ruin of Judea, which he compares to the cutting down of a forest; by which he means that there is nothing so valuable that the enemies will not destroy it, till they have stripped the whole land of its ornaments.
And Lebanon will fall violently. He mentions Lebanon, because that mountain, as we all know, was highly celebrated for fruitful and highly valuable trees. Now, if he had been speaking of the Assyrians, it would not have been appropriate to introduce the destruction of Lebanon. Hence we infer that the Prophet, in this passage, again threatens the Jews; and this agrees well with the introduction of the discourse, for it begins with a word which calls attention, Behold.
CHAPTER 11
Isaiah Chapter 11:1-16
1. And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots:
1. Sed prodibit virga ex trunco Isai; et surculus de radicibus ejus fructus edet.
2. And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the Lord;
2. Et requiescet super eum Spiritus Iehovae, spiritus sapientiae et intelligentiae, spiritus consilii et fortitudinis, spiritus scientiae et timoris Iehovae.
3. And shall make him of quick understanding in the fear of the Lord; and he shall not judge after the sight of his eyes, neither reprove after the hearing of his ears:
3. Et sagacem illum reddet in timore Iehovae; non secundum aspectum oculorum suorum judicabit, neque ex auditu aurium suarum arguet.
4. But with righteousness shall he judge the poor, and reprove with equity for the meek of the earth: and he shall smite the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips shall he slay the wicked.
4. Nam judicabit in justitia pauperes, et in aequitate arguet mansuetis terrae; et percutiet terram virga oris sui, et spiritu labiorum suorum interficiet impium.
5. And righteousness shall be the girdle of his loins, and faithfulness the girdle of his reins.
5. Et erit justitia balteus lumborum ejus, et fides balteus renum ejus.
6. The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the calf, and the young lion, and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them.
6. Habitabit lupus cum agno, et pardus cum hoedo accubabit; vitulus, et leo, et pecus pingue pariter; et puer parvus reget eos.
7. And the cow and the bear shall feed; their young ones shall lie down together: and the lion shall eat straw like the ox.
7. Vacca et ursus pascentur; simul accubabunt foetus eorum. Et leo, quasi bos, comedet paleas.
8. And the sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice’ den.
8. Et oblectabitur infans super foramine aspidis; et super speluncam cerastis qui ablactatus est manum suam mittet.
9. They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain: for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.
9. Non nocebunt, neque injuriam inferent in toto monte sanctitatis meae; quoniam impleta erit terra scientia Iehovae, tanquam aquis mare operientibus.
10. And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek: and his rest shall be glorious.
10. Et erit in die illa, Radix Isai, quae stabit in signum populorum, requiretur a Gentibus, et erit requies ejus gloria.
11. And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.
11. Et erit in die illa, adjiciet Dominus rursus manum suum ad possidendas reliquias populi sui, quae residuae erunt ab Assur, et ab AEgypto, a Parthia, ab Arabia, ab AEthiopia, a Perside, a Chaldaea, ab Hamath, et ab insulis maris.
12. And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.
12. Et levabit signum Gentibus, congregabitque ejectos Israel, et dispersiones Iuda congregabit a quatuor plagis terrae.
13. The envy also of Ephraim shall depart, and the adversaries of Judah shall be cut off: Ephraim shall not envy Judah, and Judah shall not vex Ephraim.
13. Et abscedet aemulatio Ephraim, et hostes Iuda excidentur. Ephraim non aemulabitur Iuda, nec Iuda anget Ephraim.
14. But they shall fly upon the shoulders of the Philistines toward the west; they shall spoil them of the east together: they shall lay their hand upon Edom and Moab; and the children of Ammon shall obey them.
14. Involabunt autem in humeros Philistinorum ad occidentem; diripient pariter filios orientis, AEdom et Moab missio manus eorum, et filii Ammon obedientia eorum.
15. And the Lord shall utterly destroy the tongue of the Egyptian sea; and with his mighty wind shall he shake his hand over the river, and shall smite it in the seven streams, and make men go over dry-shod.
15. Et in nihilum rediget Iehova linguam maris AEgypti; et eriget manum suam super fluvium in fortitudine venti sui; et percutiet illum in septem rivis, et faciet calcari cum calceamentis.
16. And there shall be an highway for the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria; like as it was to Israel in the day that he came up out of the land of Egypt.
16. Et erit semita reliquiis populi ejus, quae residuae erunt ab Assur, quemadmodum fuit Israel, in die qua ascendit e terra AEgypti.
